text:
I declare open this hearing of the Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Legislation Committee into the 2026-27 supplementary budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders past, present and emerging. I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in the room here today.

The committee has fixed Thursday 17 December 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee's proceedings today will begin with the corporate matters outcome of the Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry portfolio. Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It's also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate orders specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. I incorporate the public immunity statement into Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I now welcome Senator the Hon. Anthony Chisholm, Assistant Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, representing the Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry. Minister, do you wish to make an opening statement?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: No, thanks.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I welcome Ms Victoria Anderson, Secretary of the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry. Ms Anderson, do you wish to make an opening statement?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
I do have a brief opening statement. We recently tabled our 2025-26 annual report, which gives an overview of the breadth of work we have undertaken over the past year. I am sure we will be discussing much of this throughout today's proceedings, but I did want to take this opportunity to highlight some significant areas of work.

Since we last appeared before the committee, the department has responded to the first detections and ongoing outbreak of H5 bird flu in Australia. The preparedness work we have undertaken over the past two years with the Commonwealth, state and territory government colleagues and industry has positioned us well to respond. When H5 was detected in Australia, we moved quickly to activate response plans and support a coordinated response. We have engaged closely with stakeholders from government and industry as well as environmental and wildlife organisations. We have communicated carefully with the public, ensuring people have adequate access to information without being unduly worried. Targeted vaccination is being used to help protect priority native species. This globally significant rollout is supported by expert scientific advice and is being delivered on the ground by states and territories and their partners. Thankfully, there has not yet been a spillover into the poultry industry, but we know from overseas experience that this is still a risk, and across governments and industry we continue to focus on preparedness.

I want to acknowledge the extraordinary effort of departmental staff working on this response. Many have been working under intense pressure for several months. Their professionalism, expertise and commitment helped us respond quickly and with authority. I also acknowledge the work of our state and territory colleagues and the many other partners that have contributed to the response.

The conflict in the Middle East also continues to affect Australia's agriculture, fisheries and forestry industries. The immediate pressures have changed over time, but they have not disappeared. Higher input and transport costs continue to affect producers and supply chains. Of course, we now are in a period of high demand for diesel as the grain harvest is underway across the country. We continue to monitor fuel and fertiliser supply, prices and distribution and to work with industry and other parts of government to identify pressure points and respond to emerging issues. Our ongoing engagement with producers, exporters, suppliers and logistics businesses has helped us understand the impacts across different industries and regions.

Both H5 bird flu and the conflict in the Middle East have demonstrated the importance of preparation, partnerships and being able to quickly bring together technical, economic and operational expertise. The department has played an important leadership role in both responses. We welcome the committee's questions.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I will invite questions on corporate matters. Senator Canavan.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I have some questions on ANAO report No. 4, released in May, about biosecurity pricing. How much biosecurity cost recovery revenue has DAFF collected? How much was spent, and what was the surplus in each of the last three financial years?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think our CFO will take this question.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: For the last three years in the biosecurity arrangements, I will start with 2022-23. Total revenue was $364 million; total expenses were $351 million, with an accumulated deficit of $6.8 million. In 2024-25, total revenue was $428 million; total expenses were $408 million, with a surplus of $13.6 million. Sorry, that is the accumulated result. I will come back to the accumulated deficit. Then, for 2025-26, the total revenue was $466 million and total expenses were $453 million.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: As the ANAO report found, there have been surpluses recovered here. Why are farmers being overcharged, then, for these services at the moment?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Firstly, it is mostly not farmers who are paying these fees; it is importers. I want to clarify that. We do not budget to either over- or underrecover expenditure that is cost recovered from industry. The department sets prices consistent with the government policy, and in most cases this is the cost estimated to fully recover for the provision of regulatory services. Our assumptions to calculate prices can change during the financial year. That can result in surpluses or deficits. We have had both over the last four or five years, and this is normal. We do try to minimise variances wherever possible, but where there are unforeseen fluctuations it's often because we've taken time to staff up to the levels required to deliver the services rather than anything else. Mr Geysen may want to add to that.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Seconding what the secretary has said, we have had that significant growth in revenue over the past couple of years, in particular with the implementation of the self-assessed clearances. For 2025-26 compared to 2023-24, that has added another $60 million worth of revenue to the biosecurity arrangement. For us to be able to respond to that growth, we receive or invoice in arrears, so understanding the demand and being able to respond to that and staff up to that does take time.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
I understand the evidence you provide is you do not intend to overcharge. I suppose the issue is the Auditor-General found:

DAFF is not managing the risk of under- or over-recovery.

Do you agree with that conclusion, and, if so, why were you not managing the risk of this occurring?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We do welcome the ANAO's report. It has been very valuable. We have accepted the need to continue to strengthen our cost recovery administration and have taken steps to address most of the findings already. The audit covered a period several years ago, and obviously that has given us a chance to improve since then. The report does not suggest the department is failing to deliver regulatory services but does point, as you have said, to opportunities to improve how costs are measured, documented, governed and reflected in charges.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Can I come back to my question. I am not so sure it is fair to say 'several years ago'; 2024-25 is not that long ago. Why was the department not managing the risk of under- or overrecovery?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think the ANAO was encouraging us to increase the level of oversight of that risk. We do look at cost recovery on a monthly basis. It gets reported through our relevant governance channels. What the ANAO has suggested is that we formally embed that risk, for example, in divisional business plans, taking it to a level below what we previously had, managing it as an enterprise risk down to lower levels of the business.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Of the overrecovery that has occurred in each of the last three years, how much has been paid by farmers?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I do not think we would have that breakdown, because the cost is applied to the importer. Sometimes that may be a farmer, but mostly it is a business importing food or other products that we inspect at the border. So it will be a range of different—
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It's in the supply chain too.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It's in the supply chain, correct.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Some of these costs will be borne by farmers?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes, some of it will be.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: How do you propose to make good here, given you have overcharged? Are they going to get a subsidy going forward or a rebate to reflect overcharging?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Obviously, a surplus usually will go into our cash reserves and then manage a deficit position going forward. We manage that over a number of years. Mr Geysen may want to correct me if I get this wrong, but I think our goal is not to overrecover, of course, but we also—
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: But there has been overrecovery of some.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: There has been—and underrecovery prior to that, as Mr Geysen said.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Over the last few years—and, obviously, the problem for the individual businesses is they are not necessarily the same ones who have been under- and overrecovered—it looks like something close to $50 million of overrecovery. Are any of these businesses going to get a refund?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: No, they won't. The charges were correctly applied according to the policy, as we described. The individual services were not overcharged. It's our estimate of how much business could be—
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It's overrecovery. Isn't it meant to be cost recovery? If you have charged them more than your costs, that's overcharging, isn't it?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think it is the difference between any individual cost, which is not overrecovery, but in our estimates of aggregate costs—
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: But any of these businesses in the supply chain, if they overcharge their customers, will have to give them the money back. That would be under the law. Why is the same law not applied to the government?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: As far as I am aware, there is nothing under the charging framework that prevents that. If we were to go down that path, we need—
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Are you a law unto yourself?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
No. We have a cost recovery maturity program at the moment that we have established this year. As Mr Geysen said, there are a range of different oversight mechanisms that we want to apply into the system. There's no perfect science for cost recovery. We are always acting with imperfect information based on last year's volumes, for example. There will be fluctuations from year to year. If you looked at a longer period, you would find that we were underrecovering as well. We can't select a particular set of years and say that we're overcharging and another set of years and say, 'That's fine, because we undercharged.' We look at this as a system.

We're taking a systems response in terms of responding to the auditors. It does not mean individuals have been charged more than the cost of issuing a certificate, for example, or something like that. It just means we have not a hundred per cent accurately estimated how much the delivery of those services will cost in any given financial year. What we hope is that over time there are robust systems to show that we have delivered the services and delivered them adequately. There is no system that is going to mean we hit a zero-dollar balance on any cost recovery program at the end of the financial year, because we are acting on last year's information to set the prices for the following year.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Was the aggregate surplus about $26 million?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Correct. At the end of 2025-26, in terms of the biosecurity arrangement, yes, it's $26.02 million.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Do you target to underrecover this year to make that up?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: No, we're not permitted to underrecover.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: But you can overrecover?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: In aggregate, yes, and we can underrecover in aggregate as well.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: That seems very strange. Where is this $26 million? Is it in a bank account?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It sits as cash reserves. We're not allowed to reprioritise it and use it for other things.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We overrecovered last year, so we will at least target to be $26 million under this year; you can't do that?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: No.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: To get that gone, you have to accidentally underrecover?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We could also take decisions to expend that money on things that reduce costs over time. For example, I mentioned the cost-recovery improvement program. One of the things I have asked the team to do within the rules is look at, if we do have a surplus, whether we use a proportion of that to improve the ICT systems that are used in order to drive down costs going forward, for example. That may be a bad example, because it is not operating costs; it is capital. Those are the sorts of things we are looking at through this cost-recovery improvement program.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: But on the numbers you have just given on the recovery, there has been almost a 15 per cent or 14 per cent increase year on year. That is triple inflation. How is cost recovery driving productivity when you—

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It is about the volume. Volumes of imports have increased, and therefore we collect more money. It is not about our deciding to charge more.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Is there a metric where you look at volume per box, per tonne or per whatever to look at those efficiencies? Is that in the report?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I will defer to Mr Geysen on how we do our projections, but we do look at past performance and volumes. Volumes have astronomically gone up over the last few years.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: That's correct. Every year we are required to go through a process to evaluate the prices heading into next year before we go up to consultation with industry. Through the last cost-recovery implementation statement, we did a comprehensive review of the biosecurity charges to look at not only what indexation should be applied to it but also what other charges should either be modified or adjusted within that process as well. It's nearly a checkpoint in the year to ensure those fees and prices heading into next year reflect the volumes as the secretary has said.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: In short, our over- or underrecovery is usually due to an inability of us to accurately project the volume as opposed to anything else.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
That's a good segue, though, to this issue of your costs, because perhaps the most damning finding in this report was, as I will quote from the Auditor-General:

Although DAFF has established a charging model, it could not demonstrate that the prices it sets reflect actual or minimum efficient costs, and its charging model was not applied consistently in setting prices.

I am particularly interested in the finding there that the prices do not reflect minimum efficient costs. Do you agree with that conclusion?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think there's an opportunity to demonstrate that we are going down to that level. If I take a step back, we track prices at what we call an output level. To be able to meet the expectations of the ANAO when it's assessing minimum efficient cost, they have recommended that you go down to the next level, or a business process level. We have now implemented a process where we have a rolling program of activity-based costings to go and assess at that business process level. It is fair to say, though, when you do put the effort into tracking costs at a more granular level, there are administration costs that come with that as well. It is a balancing act for us to find what that minimum efficient cost is.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: But you do not disagree that at the moment you cannot tell us that the $453 million in costs for 2025-26 are the minimum efficient costs?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: From what I have seen and the processes and the controls that we have around our cost-recovery processes, the annual reviews that we undertake through those costs, in our view we are operating at minimum efficient cost.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: You disagree with the Auditor-General?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think there is more that we can do to demonstrate that.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: To me, this has been a constant complaint in this committee for years, reflecting the views of industry, that they have not had a proper oversight here, and they question whether or not there has been an attempt to cross-subsidise. I will get to that. The Auditor-General is effectively vindicating industry's views here, but I still see intransigence from the department saying, 'There's nothing to see here. We're fine. We're at minimum efficient costs.' What is it going to take for industry to have their view if you just ignore the Auditor-General?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
It is definitely not our evidence to say there is nothing to see here. As I said, we have a cost-recovery improvement program. I think it has been one thing I have heard, both on the import and the export side, most from industry since I started as secretary. I don't want anyone to think we are taking this lightly. We have agreed with all the ANAO recommendations. We started addressing them well before the ANAO report landed with us in the middle of the year. I agree with you. It's a really important issue to get right. It's a really important issue to demonstrate to industry that they can have trust in the fees that we are providing, and we do have a range of processes internally to improve.

In terms of that issue of over- and underrecovery that you have touched on, it is very difficult under the current guidance that we follow from Finance to be able to absolutely accurately predict, because we are just dealing with a demand-driven set of situations. It is not an excuse but a reality of how we set these things up. We are doing our best to be as open and transparent as possible. We talk to industry oversight groups quite regularly about this on the biosecurity side. That is chaired by Deputy Secretary Saunders. We are definitely not a closed book, and we definitely do not think it is job done. There is a fair bit of work still to do.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: You said that you have agreed with the recommendations, but recommendation No. 1 of the report from the Auditor-General is that 'the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry improve visibility and monitoring of the minimum efficient cost of key business processes required to deliver its outputs'. DAFF's response is 'agreed in principle'—not fully agreed. Why haven't you fully agreed with that recommendation?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think the recommendation is around improving visibility and monitoring. As Mr Geysen said, we agree with that. We don't necessarily agree with the idea that we're overcharging or not charging or doing our best to charge the minimum efficient cost. It's how we demonstrate that. As Mr Geysen said, there is a balance, because if we go down to a certain level of detail it will add costs for industry as we will be tracking and monitoring at different points in the process. Ultimately, that will add costs. We are conscious that, in order to demonstrate some of these things, what we don't want inadvertently to do is charge people more for the pleasure. We are definitely agreeing in principle, but it is about how we execute that we are giving careful thought to it so it does not add costs.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I take the point you are trying to make. The problem is you are a monopoly and people do not have any other alternative. Every other business regulated in this way through infrastructure charging principles and the like has to do this. They do building blocks; they have to go through this. I do not understand why you think you should be exempt from similar scrutiny. Yes, it will add a cost, but the problem is, without that additional work being done, we cannot have assurance. We effectively have to take you on trust, and you are in a conflicted position. I have made this point many times. You have a conflict. You would like to, obviously, charge more money, and the department and the government would like to be able to cross-subsidise the fees charged to importers, to producers, to offset the costs of the broader government. I am still hearing that you do not believe you should face the same scrutiny as any other natural monopoly in this country that would face pricing principles?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think we do face a fair bit of scrutiny. The ANAO has just looked at us. As I said, we have industry asking questions, with the opportunity to ask questions very regularly through the consultative bodies that we have in place. We certainly do not disagree that we have a job to do to demonstrate to industry that we are delivering the minimum efficient costs, but I do think there are a range of different ways we could go about this. That is what we are looking into. It is not a done deal. We have not answered that question yet. We are going through the process right now.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
DAFF quotes that you conducted three reviews of your charging model in 2024. It says:

The reviews identified risks related to the accuracy of DAFF's cost estimates and prices.

Are those reviews publicly available?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: No.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: On notice, could we get copies of those three reviews referred to by the Auditor-General. The problem here is those reviews apparently identified risks, yet nothing seems to have been done, or at least not done to assuage the conclusions here of the Auditor-General. Why were those three reviews not acted upon sufficiently to avoid such a damning report from the Auditor-General?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think they were acted upon. We were not able to include some of those actions in the audit report because they put a time boundary around when they were looking at it. The things we have done, for example most of last year and into this year, were not necessarily reflected in that ANAO report, and that's fine; that's how they are done. It is certainly not true to say that actions were not done in response to earlier concerns raised as we went through the audit process in response to things that we knew the auditors were looking at and that we needed to improve.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: The report also found that the department had failed to advise both the secretary and the minister that some of its prices were not directly informed by its charging model. When did the secretary and the minister realise that some of the prices set weren't directly informed by the charging model?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think I will defer to others. That was prior to my time.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think that was prior to my time. In making that recommendation, we understand that the Auditor-General said that it was 34 per cent of prices that were not aligned. That represents about three per cent of our biosecurity cost-recovered revenue. The corrections made at that time were to ensure there was no overcharging. The adjustments made to the prices at that time were to ensure the correct charge was passed on to industry.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
Can you take on notice when the minister and secretary were informed that had occurred. The next sentence in the Auditor-General's report says:

DAFF's ability to effectively manage the risk of cross subsidisation is limited.

That has been one of my major complaints here. What are you doing to ensure there is no risk of cross-subsidisation?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think that stems from the ANAO's recommendation around how we use our effort-based cost drivers. We articulate and we go through a process where we look at the effort to inform the allocation of costs. We are currently going through the process of implementing a new activity-based costing piece of software at the current point to replace our legacy one, which will go to increasing our ability to ensure the accuracy of effort allocated to cost recovered arrangements.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Senator Colbeck.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: In terms of those charges and costings, when did you get the draft report from the ANAO which was issued in July? When did you get the draft, which would have given you the opportunity to comment?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We can just find that information for you. We found it through the section 19 process. We will just check on the date for that and come back. From memory, it was within a month or so of when it was finalised.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think it was mid-May, but I will get the exact date, because then we have 28 calendar days to be able to respond to the draft report.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: That's fine. I want to go to one particular area of costs. The acronym I have here is 'SAC', which is for—

text: Yes, of course.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
Australia, effectively, prior to the conflict imported about 60 per cent of its urea from the Middle East, and that travelled via the Strait of Hormuz. As soon as the conflict arose, that supply chain was effectively interrupted and that source was effectively unavailable. You would be aware that the timing of that conflict was leading into the winter planting season. Urea, which is the dominant form of fertiliser required for Australian production systems—because we're effectively nitrogen poor in our Australian soils—meant that the timing that we need that urea was effectively when we were short of urea as well due to that conflict. There are a couple of other dynamics that were occurring in the global market as a result of that. One of the dynamics was obviously a range of other countries also need urea. India, for example, were putting out significant tenders for large amounts of urea, which meant there was significant global competition for urea supplies as well. In addition, some other countries that supply urea or are net exporters of urea also effectively put export controls on urea as well. I think China was one of those. You can see that the whole market effectively contracted at a time when Australia really needed urea. There were a couple of things that the Australian government did in response to that situation. The first was to look at alternative markets for the supply of urea to where we would normally obtain them. Obviously, I said the Middle East was a particular dependency for Australia. We worked closely with DFAT and with the Department of Industry, Science and Resources to identify alternative markets. Those markets were South-East Asia, so near neighbours, but also Africa as well, and countries in Africa. What's really encouraging and cause for optimism is that, as a result of the conflict, the diversification of our imports of urea has significantly expanded as a consequence of the work that government did with industry to identify some of those alternative suppliers and markets.

In addition, the government established the fuel and fertiliser security facility. That facility effectively was a facility to support industry to obtain urea supplies that were additional to what they would otherwise be able to obtain on commercial terms in the international market. I talked about some of those dynamics that were existing in the international market. In addition, the urea price globally increased from around US$500 a tonne to around US$900 a tonne, a significant increase. There was a greater risk in terms of obtaining those shipments on the international market for commercial entities. That facility was established and a number of companies were effectively signed up under that facility.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: As the secretary mentioned, the Regional Investment Corporation is an important source of support with concessional loans. There are a number of supports.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: That's good. Why is continuity of service important during a period of conflict related cost pressures?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Ultimately, it's about food security, and that's why we're working on a food security strategy. Ultimately, food security is something that underpins the security of this nation. It underpins the security of this region. We recognise that the agriculture sector is subject to a range of different shocks that are challenging to prepare for—it's not that the sector doesn't prepare for those—such as drought. A Middle East conflict is less foreseeable.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes, they've got enough to worry about as it is, the poor devils, haven't they? So, if we can ease any of the pain, this is great news. Lastly, how do you get that message out? How does DAFF get the message out to farmers and farmer groups that all of this is available should they need it?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We're engaged with the sector constantly and across the organisation, but what is, I think, really important, and something that the minister established, for example, during the Middle East crisis and has continued, was an industry roundtable. It was meeting, I think, fortnightly.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It started weekly.
witness_organisation: Office of the Chief Plant Protection Officer

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It started weekly. That brought together industry stakeholders from across Australia, where they could receive a briefing from the minister and the secretary. We had the Australian Institute of Petroleum, the NFF and Fertiliser Australia as well. There was a dissemination of information. What industry told us was that peak industry organisations then used that briefing to disseminate out to their members, farmers on the ground in a lot of cases. Trying to just get that information flow happening and keep that information flow happening was a key focus for us.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I've done the normal Senate estimates thing there. I've lied; it's not my last question. I've just got to go back on this, and I can't stress this enough to whoever is listening: the power of consultation with industry. Roundtables—I've held a few myself—are a magnificent opportunity for industry to get into the minds of the bureaucracy and the bureaucracy to hear from industry, to say that we're not opposed to each other, 'You've got your expertise here; we've got ours, and if you listen to us and we work with you, it's amazing what we can achieve together.' And we're not draining the coffers of the Treasury.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I wholeheartedly agree. Some of these challenges are significant, and I think government working on its own, industry working on its own, is not going to achieve as much as both working together.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

text: Maybe I could answer the question more broadly. What we were conscious of is that it was an extraordinary intervention in the market and it was done so in the national interest. So having more of Australia's companies out on the global market chasing fertiliser in the interests of Australian producers was exactly what we wanted. However, in a resource constrained environment, what we needed to do was tranche the companies that EFA engaged with to sign them up, and that was very much a starting point for EFA as well, given they were also doing the fuel facility at the same time as well.

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

text: Returning to the eligibility criteria that we used, they were effectively also a way for us to think about how we prioritised referrals of companies. Incitec Pivot and CSBP are acknowledged large importers of urea to Australia. witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I'd also add the design around retrospective shipments as well. I wouldn't categorise it necessarily as a queue of companies or that sort of thing. text: Did you assess the losses to importers and resellers who were not included? Industry has estimated that there is an estimated loss to importers and resellers who were not included of between $20 million and $25 million. Have you conducted your own analysis in that regard?

text: No.

text: Those losses flow from government's intervention in the market. Have you considered how that should be addressed?

text: Our response at last estimates was that this is an unprecedented intervention, as Mr Lowe indicated. We are not aiming to be in this market any longer than we thought we needed to be. The facility is paused, as we've indicated, and it's paused because the uncertainty in the situation means it could turn quickly and we want to be ready to act. agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Secretary, farmers and working holiday-makers, colloquially known as backpackers, have been unfairly included in a political campaign to cut overseas migration. I expect you're aware that the Labor government has promised to cut very soon the rate of backpackers to almost 50 per cent of what they currently are over any three-year period. Was the department of agriculture consulted in respect of those changes before that promise was announced?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes, we were.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: What did those consultations involve?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We participated in the usual way. Obviously, this is led by Minister Burke's portfolio and the Department of Home Affairs. As the various policy propositions were put, our department was involved in that. Ultimately, cabinet processes were involved and we participated in that in the usual way, through coordination comments on exposure drafts and submissions—those sorts of things. We're also very aware of the issue that a range of industries, particularly horticulture, have raised around the impact on their industries. We've participated in a range of different consultations with industry representatives as well throughout that process.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Did you collate recommendations in respect of the proposed changes and present them to the minister for immigration or his department?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Your position, or the position of the department that you represent, has in one place its position on the proposed cuts to backpackers?

text: That would be subject to cabinet processes and restrictions on information, but, yes, we have in one place, I guess—that's Mr Lowe's group in our department, and I think Mr Blong's division is responsible for looking at workforce issues across agriculture, so, yes, that's certainly the case.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think we'd have to check. There would be minutes of those meetings and things like that, so there would be other documents relating to workforce issues in agriculture, most definitely, especially over time. witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Please do now formally take that on notice. What is the department's position on the cuts to the rates of backpackers for our agricultural industry?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Maybe I can add to the secretary's comments. With those whole-of-government processes, where we provide advice into a whole-of-government process, ultimately government makes a decision, and that is a policy decision. Departments in and of themselves don't have positions, if you like. We're subject to whole-of-government policy and policy decisions of government. We administer that policy. In relation to this particular instance, what I would just, I guess, in addition offer is that we're cognisant of the role the Working Holiday Maker program plays for the agriculture sector. We're aware of a range of different purposes through which it's used, particularly, for example, for the horticulture sector but also in the grains industry as well. It's important for us to engage with the sector and understand how they might see some of the implications for changes to that program. It's important for us, in terms of having our own knowledge and information around that, to feed that through to the lead agency where that's appropriate, and that's Home Affairs, and that's what we do.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I'm not sure how long you've had that position, Mr Lowe, but you may in any event recall the COVID days and the impact that it had on the production of fruit and vegetables across Australia and the significant price increase that followed from that. That was in circumstances where there was plenty of produce rotting in the ground because we simply did not have the necessary number of people to undertake harvests. So do you agree that the COVID days and the impact that it had on the agricultural industry is a good comparison to the situation that we will soon be in following the cuts to the rates of backpackers?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I don't think that's accurate, and when you look at the numbers that we are aiming to get to on the working holiday-makers, it is back to where we were pre-COVID. There's been a 64 per cent increase since that time. So I think, in terms of the numbers that we're looking at as part of our projections, it is getting back to that pre-COVID level. We understand there's obviously ongoing discussion with industry, as the department have talked about, which is going to be really important about how we manage these issues. We also recognise the important role the PALM scheme plays, and there has been great success about how that scheme has worked in recent years in terms of the number of people coming in, working in agriculture and the meat industry as well, and we are in ongoing discussion with Minister Burke's office—and so is industry—about how these changes are implemented to ensure that we can manage this as best as possible.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Senator Chisholm, can you please repeat your answer in respect of comparing what the situation will be following the cut to backpackers to what the situation was for our agricultural sector at the time of COVID?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: The point I was making was that the numbers that we want to get to on working holiday-makers is where the country was at pre-COVID. We want to get back to those numbers from before COVID hit. There has been a 64 per cent increase since. We want to get back to those numbers that were pre-COVID.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Doesn't it follow, though, that if our agricultural industry is not going to be able to achieve harvest at its ordinary rate, following the cuts to backpackers, that we simply are producing more food and we simply need to maintain the number of backpackers so we can meet our current production rates?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I don't think that's accurate. What I talked through is the numbers that we want to get to. We understand the importance of working holiday-makers for our agriculture sector. We're engaging with those representatives from those industries. I know that there are ongoing conversations with Minister Burke's office as well about how these issues are handled to ensure that we have the workforce where we need it, when we need it.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: What will you do to support farmers who are negatively affected by the cuts to the rates of backpackers? I will give you an example. Most recently, I was talking to one of the largest producers of potatoes in Tasmania. He produces 25,000 tonnes of potatoes every year; 90 per cent of the people who harvest those potatoes are backpackers. He can't fill those jobs with Aussies. He needs backpackers. He assures me that he will not be able to fulfil his harvest and there will be more than half of his potential potato crop left rotting in the ground. What are you going to do to help farmers who are ending up in a position like that because of the rates of cuts to backpackers?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: What we are doing is managing the NOM to get down to the levels that we indicated. We've also said that we want to have the working holiday-maker numbers back to where they were pre COVID, where we've seen a 64 per cent increase. We are committed to working with industry to ensure that we get the workers where they are needed for harvest. That's our commitment. That's what we're working with industry to achieve. The ongoing engagement with Minister Burke is an important part of that.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I put it to you that, if we want to work with industry to give them the workers that they need to do their job and provide us with the food that we need, it will involve not cutting the rates of backpackers. Will you consider doing everything within your power to ensure that we do not follow through on a cut to the rates of backpackers because of the significant adverse impact that it is going to have on our agricultural industry across this country?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: What we are committed to is getting to the NOM of 225,000 people, managing the working holiday-makers so that we can get down to those pre-COVID levels and ensuring that we can get the workers where they need to be for harvest. That's what we're working to achieve.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: So you're working to an archaic target, a pre-COVID target, where times have changed and what our farmers need now differs from what they needed then. Is that what your evidence is today?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: No, I don't think that's an accurate reflection. I think the other thing that you need to consider is the work we've been doing around the PALM scheme and the 28,000 Australians who have enrolled in fee-free TAFE in the agricultural area. There are a range of other measures that we've been putting in place to ensure that we can be well placed to have the workforce where we need it, when we need it.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

That was one of the issues that we were raising with Treasury, as we did our own analysis about what impacts that might have and fed that to Treasury as part of their considerations.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: So, as a result of these tax changes, will some farms potentially lose access to farm management deposits if they change their structure?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I guess, as I mentioned before, the application of the changes to businesses will depend on the individual circumstances of those businesses. Since the budget has come out, a number of changes to the proposal have been encapsulated in the exposure draft, and they have the impact of increasing the options available to farm businesses to be able to react to the changes in a way that is best or optimised for their business, I suppose. One of those has been those partial rollover arrangements, which allow farm businesses to remove the non-primary production assets and incomes from the discretionary trust structure. The reason for that is that, for eligibility for farm management deposits, trusts and companies aren't able to hold farm management deposits. I guess the consideration was that, if farmers were incentivised to move their primary production assets out of discretionary trusts as a result of the changes, they wouldn't be able to access the scheme. That was one of the considerations in providing the option for farmers to be able to keep their primary production assets within a discretionary trust structure, as that allows them to still be eligible for farm management deposits. That is because the income from those primary production activities would remain in that structure.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We might just take a step back, because this sounds incredibly confusing. Is that the basic issue?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: That's correct. Companies and trusts are ineligible to hold farm management deposits, and the reason for that comes back to scheme integrity. There's a cap on the amount that an individual can hold in farm management deposits, and having companies or trusts eligible for that makes it very hard to enforce that cap, whereas we are able to do that with individuals.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: That's correct, yes.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: So, with the changes announced in the budget, there was an expectation in the budget and specific discussion about the fact that some businesses would seek to change to a corporate structure from a trust structure. agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: If it took its whole business, including those assets that are related to primary production income; if it completely removed those assets and restructured its business as a corporation or company, that's correct. witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes. As I say, a farm business would have a range of options, depending on its individual circumstances. If indeed it does structure its business through a discretionary trust—as you've said, it's around 20 per cent—it has the option to maintain the entirety of its business within that discretionary trust, noting that the primary production income within that trust is exempt from the minimum 30 per cent taxation arrangements. It also has the option of partially rolling over, so removing the non-primary production assets from the discretionary trust structure and keeping the primary production assets within there. Indeed, an excluded election trust arrangement has been included in the exposure draft, and that would allow the farm business to maintain all of the assets within the discretionary trust structure and, for each of the beneficiaries, nominate a fixed proportion of the distributions from that fund and also the ownership of the assets within that fund. So there's essentially a few different—
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: As for that last one, what happens if they need to change the beneficiaries?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Senator, I should just caution you that we're probably reaching the edges of our understanding of the tax system and tax changes, but we'll go with you for as long as we can.

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I would go back to the previous point, which is that it's a scheme integrity measure. As I say, there's a cap on the amount of funds that can be held within farm management deposits for an individual, and I believe that's $800,000. text: We must welcome you to the RRAT committee, Senator Bleyer, as a full-time member. Senator Bleyer.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: What I have talked through was our aim of where we want to get to on the NOM figure, as that does have an impact on working holiday-makers. witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
I've spoken to a number of forestry professionals, including some that are involved in carbon projects now, both here on the mainland and in Tassie. It's a reasonable rainfall—it's over 600 millimetres, which is pretty good—but the soil types and the structure is of a concern, and every one that I've spoken to, every single professional forester that I've spoken to about this, talks about this having an MAI of 10 to 15 cubic metres per hectare per year, which was described to me by one forester who's actively involved in this here in New South Wales as non-commercial. And that's because of the structure of the site.

I'm genuinely concerned about the capacity for this project to deliver, based on this very qualified advice that I've had. There's a bloke up in that region who has a business taking out failed plantations because of the attributes of the location of the region. That's his business. So how do we have confidence in this project when the documents that I've received talk about 3.2 million tonnes of CO2 being provided as a part of it, but an MAI of 15 is not going to get anywhere near that? How do we understand that we're getting what we're paying for, which goes to the point why I'm asking all those questions about how you assess the project, if the MAI has been considered so low? This is what one of the foresters has said to me: 10 to 15, which is about a third to a half of a productive plantation on good soil with rainfall above 600 millimetres. The soil is sand over clay, so that's why it's so good for irrigated pasture, because you're effectively using aquaponics. It's irrigated, as we know. The trees will dry out the sand layer; the roots won't penetrate the heavy clay, which is relatively shallow. If there's heavy rain, the trees will be sitting on swampy ground, which cools the root systems, and then they have to try to recover, and the risk of sirex wasp infection is real as well. That's the assessment of a highly qualified professional forester in Tasmania who knows the country, and yet there's nothing in the application process that interrogates the productivity of the site in terms of either timber production or ACCUs.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: What you're pointing to is obviously someone with expertise and capability in forestry management giving you an opinion about the potential productivity of the site. We absolutely appreciate that. As Mr Bursle has outlined, the premise for the way in which we require information from proponents is the same: a forest management professional who is highly qualified undertaking a detailed assessment of the site and providing that assurance back to the department that the project offers a productive and economic investment. I guess it's in no-one's interests, including the proponent's, for the project to fail as well. So there are a range of different checks and balances that we put in place to assure ourselves.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: But I'm genuinely concerned that there have been no checks and balances. It's not just one forester that's told me this, it's three or four who are Tasmanians who understand the country and know what's going on. The taxpayer is a 50 per cent or 49 per cent shareholder in this project. We're told we'll get a return, and yet the information that I'm being given is that it's not commercial. So what is the return?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I'm going to have to share the call around. We've been quite generous. Do you want to just answer that question? You don't want to answer it?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: People who know the country are telling me, and not just one—several of them.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: In September 2025, the Australian government released Australia's national climate risk assessment, and in that document it found that the current climate risk to the primary industries and food system is rated moderate to high. Coincidentally, I'm sure, in the same month—also in September 2025—the Department of Climate Change released its National adaptation plan, and in that document it says the risk of climate change to primary industries that decreases productivity, quality and profitability and increases biosecurity pressures is currently rated as moderate. So we've got two federal government reports produced in the same month of the same year, being September last year, one of which rates the risk of climate change to primary industry at moderate to high and the other which rates it at moderate. So which policy are you implementing in the department of agriculture?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I'm familiar with those reports, and I guess the industry itself would recognise it as being a highly climate-exposed sector.
witness_organisation: Office of the Chief Plant Protection Officer

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: A highly what, I'm sorry?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: A climate exposed sector, in terms of the impacts of climate change and having to adapt to those impacts. It's a sector, both through the R&D system, that has invested levy payer and obviously Commonwealth matching funds through addressing some of those challenges around the impacts of climate change across all sectors—livestock and cropping and beyond. There's also a number of government programs which the department administers that go to this issue as well, including the Future Drought Fund, the Natural Heritage Trust funded Climate-Smart Agriculture Program and obviously the matching contributions we make to our R&D investment across the sector programs as well. The analysis that is contained in those reports you referred to I guess reinforce that the sector is exposed to climate change. That's not necessarily news, but it is something that galvanises attention around the need for the sector to adapt to climate change challenges, and it's a sector that has been long investing in that task and is supported by both levy payer funds and also government programs.
witness_organisation: Office of the Chief Plant Protection Officer

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Is the department of agriculture implementing the policy that climate change is a moderate risk or a moderate-to-high risk to our primary industries?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think a different way to think about that is this is information that farmers should be thinking about and using to manage the risk on their own enterprises. As Mr Blong said, this is additional information. Both the sector and ourselves are very aware that this is a climate-exposed sector. Our general principle in relation to the programs that we administer and/or the work that sits in the research and development system is about supporting farmers with the information and the tools that they can use to best manage the risks for their own enterprise and put essentially the farmer at the centre of managing that risk. So that could be in relation to drought resilience or that could be in relation to extreme weather events, but ultimately it's about ensuring that they have the tools to adapt and the information available to make the best decisions that they can.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Our farmers best respond to risks by being informed by policy implementation. Should our farmers who look to the department of agriculture consider climate change a moderate or a high risk to the industry in which they operate? Or are you, by the answers I've heard so far to the same question I'm having to put again, not prepared to tell us what policy you are implementing—whether you're implementing a moderate-risk policy or a high-risk policy—when it comes to the impact of climate change on our primary industries? It's a pretty straightforward question, I thought. But you don't want to choose between the two reports; I understand that. Just say so and I can move on.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It's information and it's analysis that we use, and also the sector uses, to inform how they adapt. I'm happy to go to my colleague to provide further commentary.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think the explanation there is that the timeframes for those two documents are different. The NCRA operates over a much longer time horizon, so the risk rating varies; it has a broader span. Whereas the NAP looks at the shorter term response, so it's the adaptation plan. I think that might explain why the risk ratings are different, but those particular pieces of work were led by the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water and also the Australian Climate Service. They would be really well placed to explain the technical differences on the risk ratings.
witness_organisation: Office of the Chief Plant Protection Officer

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: One thing that the two reports do have in common is that they both agree that the main impact on productivity is rising heat, so warming weather. Since both of these reports were published, we now have the World Meteorological Organization firmly establishing an El Nino in the tropical Pacific and the impact that it is having and will continue to have—and it's only going to get worse—on the increased heat of our weather that we are already suffering. What additional planning and economic scenario modelling has the department of agriculture done this calendar year to prepare for these and other extreme weather events so that we can protect our agricultural industry and protect domestic food security in this country?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
I think you're raising a really important issue. Again, we don't disagree with the implications of climate change for the sector, and, again, I think that is well acknowledged by the sector as well. We can have ABARES come to the table to talk about the estimates that they've done in relation to those particular climatic events that you're referring to. But perhaps more broadly, just to ground your line of questioning in the types of things that we think about and the types of analysis that we look to support the sector with, and support ourselves with as well, ABARES has done some work around climate adjusted productivity estimates that indicate that broadacre productivity growth, particularly for cropping and mixed farms, would have been materially higher under long-run average climate conditions.

Since 2000, hotter and drier conditions have reduced measured productivity growth, especially in southern cropping regions, although innovation, as Mr Blong mentioned, and adaptation by farmers have offset part of that impact. In addition, that analysis also supports that climate conditions since 2000 have reduced average annual broadacre farm profits by around 18 per cent to 23 per cent relative to what they would have been under the climate conditions experienced during 1950 to 2000. We also do work to understand how cropping regions might geographically change over the course of the next 25 years in response to changing climatic conditions as well, including hotter and drier conditions. In respect to your specific comment, what I was trying to reassure you is that we are very concerned with the implications of a changing climate for the agriculture sector. We calibrate our programs to respond to these things, but we also think it's important that ultimately farmers and farmer capability is one of the main drivers of productivity in the sector, and their ability to access up-to-date research and innovation, and that tends to be where our focus is. But I'll pass to ABARES—
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: The National Emergency Management Agency, NEMA, every year runs scenarios based on the current risks. So heat is very much factored into NEMA's work. We received a briefing on it the other day at the secretaries board that I attended. There's a range of scenarios. You mentioned the El Nino, or super El Nino as some people are calling it. That's obviously a huge concern. But actually for Australia, NEMA has done work to assess the specific risk factors affecting all parts of the country. For example, the heat scenario is quite severe. All areas are high risk for bushfire, but they've identified areas that are higher risk this season because of specific factors. There are also examples of higher propensity for rainfall and flooding events in certain parts of the country, despite the fact that we're in El Nino. How that manifests for Australia and different parts of Australia will be quite different. NEMA does appear before estimates. They would have much more detail on that, but, just to reassure you in a short-term sense, Mr Lowe has covered very well the long term. Dr Galeano can add to that. In the short term it's another part of our department, but they participate pretty strongly in that NEMA process as well, given the impact on farmers.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
