agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Obviously, we're primarily concerned with Australia's food security. One of the things that we are focused on and thinking about is, I guess, the role that Australia plays in the region as well. Just thinking about that—maybe the Middle East crisis is an instructive example in this regard—our neighbours had urea supplies and, as we discussed earlier, urea was in short supply globally. Their interest was in making that urea available to us, obviously on commercial terms, and, recognising that urea supports food production, those supplies went to our near neighbours as well. So I guess it's thinking about how those sorts of dependencies can be mutually reinforcing and support Australia's food security as a whole.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I'm asking 'how the sausage is made' just a bit, so you can tell me to sod off, but how deep do we go? When we were doing the supermarket inquiry, we noticed that one of the scopes of fresh food was the scoping and detail around the classification. They were ploughing 20 to 30 per cent of a crop that was edible but just not looking the right way back in the fields, and things like that. How far do you go with food waste: post packaging or post-sale, or pre-sale? How far are we going with stuff like that?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: To be honest, we're looking at that whole supply chain and not only what food waste happens as a result of specifications on farm but also what food waste happens as a result of, I guess, labelling requirements and, particularly, due date requirements. They are all things that have been raised with us as being worthy of consideration, which we are looking at.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We've talked about the current state of the world and looking at things through different lenses. I think you've raised the point that you're not changing your structure because of what's going on; it's the reason for it. Have you done any modelling since the outbreak of hostilities with Iran, causing us to have issues with urea and diesel? ABARE is now saying that it looks as though we'll have a positive crop again due to a whole lot of urea. How do you model that, while looking at world shocks? Are you looking at best case/worst case on these things?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It's a relatively complex area, and I'm conscious that ABARES would be better placed than us to talk about it.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Why don't they join us, Senator—I'm just looking over my shoulder—if they're the people who can answer your question?
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: In short, the answer is yes. Also, they do forecasting as part of or associated with the Australian Commodities Report.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: How do you do such forecasting? What do you put in that to model? How do you make the omelette?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We use a few different approaches, depending on the questions that we're looking at. But we're certainly looking at what's happening in current markets and futures markets for some of our inputs, as they tell us what the expectations are with what's going on and how things might play out in the next few months. We also work closely with colleagues across government. Colleagues in DCCEEW monitor it quite closely, but we also consult with colleagues in Treasury. We often think about it, though, not just in terms of fuel overall but diesel. Given its importance to agriculture, we look at diesel as well. Certainly, we've been following developments with diesel markets and refinery margins there. We take all that information and not only look for public work, like the Agricultural Commodities Report but also feed it into policy discussions, such as the food security strategy.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Again, how deep down are you going? You can dig all the way forever, but how deep are you going? Do you look at pesticide use and improvements in pesticides, fertilisers and those sorts of things? Do you look at natural improvements?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Predominantly, over the last 12 months, at least within ABARES—it might be different for other parts of the department—we've focused mainly on fertiliser and fuel. Again, we've focused not only on a lot of market input, in terms of futures prices, but also on drilling down into some of those margins that we were talking about. That would be starting with global prices and looking at various refining margins, and then trying to equate those to impacts on retail prices in Australia as well as impacts on farmers, which might be a little different.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Again, seeing that you're going there, H5 landed in Australia, and I think chicken is still the No. 1 protein in Australia. Does that factor in? That's a new threat, but did you always think it might come? How do we deal with this in the food security plan, and how do we deal with it in projections? I notice that you have said it hasn't hit poultry yet, but how many birds have been killed in America? The Americans have killed 200 million birds, or something like that, which were infected with H5.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes. We had an example with the H7 outbreak that got into chicken-and-egg production facilities last year. We did see supply chain interruptions as part of that outbreak, and that's something that's informing how we're thinking about the supply chain with H5. I guess that the decision to eradicate would be the same, regardless of disease. So we've had a bit of a dry run, I guess, with H7. In terms of that link with the food security strategy, all sorts of supply chain disruptions are possible: everything from a cyber incident down to something directly impacting production.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: You'd factor in something, but you just don't know what that something could be.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes. Also, I think we're looking at the supply chain as a whole, thinking about how you make a supply chain less vulnerable to any sort of interruption, whether it's a pest or disease outbreak, a drought, an input disruption or a supply chain or logistics sort of issue. So there's a range of different things. It's about, I guess, trying to harden those systems or looking at ways in which we might need to harden those systems to respond to a range of different threats that might be coming.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Perhaps I could just add to Ms Anderson's comments. I guess there are probably a few different lenses. There is the productive base that supports food production in Australia—farm production and those sorts of things—and then there are the supply chains, both the domestic supply chains and the international supply chains, and their resilience to shocks. That could be global shocks, biosecurity shocks, drought and those sorts of things. There are the economies in which they exist. Obviously, agriculture and food production play a vital role in regional economies as well. Then there's the lens, which I think you were touching on earlier, and that also comes through strongly around affordable, safe and healthy food so that people have access to affordable, safe and healthy food that is nutritious and they have enough of.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: My glorious party leader, who is sitting to my right, started a speech the other day while eating an apple and talking about our apple dependence. Can you remember the numbers you quoted regarding the apples?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We've gone from about 100 apples person per year to 60 in this century.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes, and that's a drop in production, not so much an increase in people, in what we do there.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: No, it's about the same production.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We've always been proud that we could feed the bowl; we could feed these people. Obviously, food security is primarily for Australia, but we're looking at what we can do as a whole department. We supply energy; we supply food. It is a very good security basis for us to be reliant. Does that feed into your program at all?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: In terms of our ability to continue to supply food to Australia's population?
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Absolutely. It is one of the principal concerns of the food security strategy. It is about being able to do that in the long run, with long-run pressures on our food production and delivery systems, as well as dealing with short-term shocks.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Given the short-term shock of specifically urea—and that was handled—have you modelled a longer term non-supply or lower supply of urea on Australian farming?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: No, I don't think we have, Senator. We're certainly thinking about a range of different scenarios that could impact Australia's food security. I don't think we've done a long-run model on urea shortage.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We haven't modelled any long-run shocks, no. Certainly, over the last few months, we've thought about what the impact on Australian agriculture would be, but not modelling a long-term increase in the urea price and a structural adjustment in agriculture.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It's not even just for how long; it's when it is, too, on seasonal stuff, isn't it? It's so important.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: One thing that's probably salient in relation to, for example, a long-term structural increase in urea price is that we are a very competitive producer of agricultural commodities globally.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Efficiency.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We're efficient and we're productive. Our farmers can afford to pay higher prices for urea in general than a lot of competing countries who produce the same commodities. While that's not ideal in terms of farmers paying an extra cost for urea, their ability to adapt, produce and still remain a going concern is something to be really proud of in a global context, and the fact that we exist in a globally competitive environment for the commodities that we produce.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Going back to the questions that Senator Cadell raised about population growth, you mentioned that you're factoring that in, but I note that, on the website for the Feeding Australia strategy, under the title 'Why we need a food security strategy', the government lists five challenges. I do say in fairness that they're not limited to these five, but the five that are highlighted are climate change, economic shocks, biosecurity threats, geopolitical factors, and supply chain disruptions. Population growth is not there, and I haven't really seen, I must say, when I looked at the discussion paper a while back, a great focus on population growth. We've had a 50 per cent increase in our population this century. It's one of the fastest in the world. Is that really being factored in here, about how we keep our food production at pace with the number of people in Australia?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: During that same period of population growth, we have still managed to export the vast majority of what we produce. I don't think there's a production problem. There've been increases in efficiency and, due to the productivity of our farmers, we've actually kept pace with that population growth domestically, such that we're still able to export.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: That's not what the data says. The volumes have gone up by about 30 per cent and the population has gone up by 50 per cent. We're not keeping pace. I totally agree with your point at the macro level. The point I've been making in speeches is that we seem to not be focused on the micro level. I think most people don't just want to know that we have enough calories; they want to have a healthy and balanced diet, and that analysis does not necessarily hold for all the parts of our food supply chain. With some commodities like apples, certainly nuts, and dairy, we're in a much more precarious position. If you take meats and grains, sure, we're way above. I just worry sometimes that we're a little bit complacent here. Are you doing that detailed analysis going down to not just a total level but also key household staples? Have we got enough to feed ourselves?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes, I think we are going down to that level. I understand the point you're making. I think that, at a macro level, I was just trying to make the point that we're still exporting the majority of what we produce, not that the proportions have increased in line with the population. I think there are a range of factors about diet, modern diet and education. There are a lot of things around how people eat and what they eat that are affecting things like the consumption of fresh fruit and vegetables that we will be looking at. Obviously, we're the department of agriculture, but the department of health and others are part of this process. There's a range of contributing factors to the modern diet that I think are part of how we're thinking about it. Historically, perhaps, it's always been pretty glib: we produce lots here. As you say, a lot of it is grain and beef, and you can't survive on that forever. We are looking to take that into a much more nuanced set of analytics about not only how food is produced—Mr Lowe has talked about those steps—but also how consumers think about food and whether there are any gaps in that area.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: There is one thing that I've struggled with, when I've looked at this closely. I must give ABARES credit: they have excellent data on the production of fresh produce—raw food, if you like. The issue I find is that the data seems a lot sparser when it comes to how we consume food through what are often packaged or processed goods. Is that something that you're trying to drill down into? Obviously, again, we have the grains and the carcasses sorted, and all these things. But in terms of converting it into a product that people buy and consume, when you go to the shops now, you can't really get tinned or canned pineapples or fruit from Australia. They're all from overseas, largely, even though we have a lot of the fresh produce. Is that being looked at as well?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: At a high level, to furnish you with some information, as we understand it, about 90 per cent of what Australians consume is domestically produced. That includes both—
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It includes processed goods?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes, it does include processed. 10 per cent is from imported, which I think is quite a privileged position for Australians, to have so much of their diets locally produced. But it is something we're concerned about. Obviously, as you'd appreciate, Senator, production and what producers choose to produce, what commodities they're in the market for, are also subject to market forces, consumption patterns and what consumers are demanding. Trying to find that balance regarding what consumers want, what we need to produce domestically and what's economic is part of the puzzle that sits in the food security strategy.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Is there any publicly available data on processed goods? That figure you used, where was that from?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I'll pass to ABARES, who are always good at supporting us with data.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: The work that we did that came up with the 90 per cent figure was work we did a few years ago. I'll probably have to check the actual source of that data. I think it was just standard import-export data, customs data. I can confirm that for you.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Okay.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It is largely processed food that we're importing. There's the odd bit of fresh out-of-season stuff, but it's mainly processed food.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I have one more question on this; then I have some stuff on the details of the strategy. There doesn't seem to be a large focus on opening up new food-growing areas. We've gone through a process where the water use in the Murray-Darling has been significantly restricted and now capped. The previous coalition government had a detailed plan to try and open up new areas of farming, particularly working with the CSIRO, and identifying water resources in Northern Australia in particular. Is any of this strategy about trying to build dams and capture new water supplies to grow more food?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It's not something we've principally concerned ourselves with, with the food security strategy. Fundamentally, one of the underpinnings, as I mentioned to Senator Cadell, is about the productive base and ensuring that base remains productive and competitive internationally.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: But how are we going to keep pace with population growth unless we build more dams and expand farming? We're going to slowly erode our food security—as we have been, and we are, right now.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I totally appreciate where you're coming from, Senator. There's a range of different inputs that support the productivity of Australian agriculture, and those drivers of productivity have meant that Australian agriculture has outperformed in terms of productivity growth—
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: A hundred per cent, it has. That's the problem, though. We've been at the frontier. Our farming sector has been one of the strongest, if not the strongest, performers at a sectoral level in terms of productivity. Despite that, as I said, with the figures that I just mentioned, we are declining in food security person, in overall time. That is despite that. I'm not sure how much faster we can expect our farmers to go when we have very high population growth. We're going to have to look, presumably, at the other side of this equation, which is the volume, the inputs. If we increase the inputs into farming, while maintaining high productivity growth, we can get more output to match population growth. I don't understand why a food security strategy doesn't focus on dams.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: You said you're looking at urea; we're looking at diesel in a lot of your forecasts, in a lot of your things in the short term. Senator Bleyer was talking about a potato farmer in Tasmania. Are you looking at your government policy now—the holiday visa, the backpackers? Have you modelled that into production?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: The purpose of our forecasts for the agricultural commodities report is that we've been following the discussion and concerns of the industry, and a lot of our forecasts are actually based on the feedback that we're hearing from industry. That is an indirect way of how we are being—
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Is that an indirect way of saying that, yes, you have factored in some change in workforce?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We're hearing what people are telling us about what the outlook looks like over the next few months. I wouldn't necessarily say that we've tied it to people, but we're aware of the challenges that people in the industry are facing. When they are saying, 'I'm thinking of doing this in the next season or over the next six months,' that's more or less what we're feeding into our projections and forecasts.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It's a very good answer. I'll try a better question. Have the people you've been talking to been saying labour force might be an issue in their plans that are coming forward?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I'd have to take that one on notice. I haven't been involved personally with some of those discussions.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: A lot of farmers are saying to us—especially the crop guys—that labour is as important as, if not more important than, some of those things across the industry. We're talking about food security. Is Australia a signatory? Are there any treaties or international devices where we have an obligation or we've signed up for food supply or food security?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I'm not aware. We can take it on notice. Not off the top of my head, Senator.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We've talked about farms; Senator Colbeck was talking about reforestation, when we're talking about international treaties on climate. I don't think we have a defensive mechanism where our responsibility to produce food is balanced against a lot of our international treaties. I don't think we have the power to reach down. If you could reach in, that would be really good.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes, we'll double-check. In terms of export, we have very few export controls or anything like that. We can double-check, in the case of an emergency. I don't want to scare people about food security in Australia, because we do produce a lot of food. Ms Hutchison, do you want to add anything on the treaty front?
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: To our knowledge, we are not signed up to anything that would commit us to that, Senator.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agricultural Trade and Regulation Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Senator, we have to be a little bit careful about commitments globally on food security, because our industry wants choice about where it sends food to. In terms of export, there are some countries who would love us to be signing up to, 'You will supply us with this, no matter what,' and we have resisted that, because our industry wants some choice. I appreciate that you're probably talking about inward food—domestic food security.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It's a little bit vexed because of the range of different interests. Some countries would have zero food security, because they don't domestically produce. We have to be a bit careful.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I was trying to subtly—now I have to do it less subtly—make a political point that international treaties can affect our agricultural lands in a negative way. I was wondering whether there was a positive way to protect them, under the same mechanism. As we go forward, are there any mechanisms, strategies or issues that are off the table, in looking at what to recommend? As an old-school protectionist Nat—I'm not going to hide that—are there any things off the table? If we say that we're suffering in an industry, can we look at supports? Could we look at help for a particular line, if it's supply lines, if it is dairy, for these things? Can we look at recommendations or particular items? Is there anything we can't recommend at this stage?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: As a general principle of policy advice that we provide to government, we do not try to contradict existing government policy.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: So you're saying milk single desk won't be in the recommendations?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I don't think so, but we have not been given any restrictions about what the strategy itself could look at. We've been told to interpret it broadly and have done so. I think the biggest restraint, personally, will be the fiscal situation. Obviously, we are operating in a constrained fiscal environment and we have to participate in a system that at the moment is not looking for giant spends. But, putting that to one side, it is a matter for government decision-making. We have not been given any riding instructions of 'Look at this' or 'Don't look at that'. It has been a very open invitation to stakeholders and then through the food council and in discussions with a range of people across government. We have not looked to restrict ourselves away from any particular topics.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I was glad you mentioned dairy, Senator, because that recently has been performing particularly well. You might have seen recent reports in the Weekly Times about farm profits being up multiple hundreds of per cent over recent years. So there's a really positive story to tell and, hopefully, that will attract more people into the industry.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Dairy farming is so hard. It is not at the bottom of jobs I would do, but it is towards the bottom. Graham Forbes would kill me if I didn't say that $2 milk should be a goal across the country.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Dairy Australia is up later today—they will have a good story to tell.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Chair, Senator Scarr has some questions.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I would like to call Senator Dolega because he has to go. Then I'll go across to Senator Scarr.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Thank you. I have some First Nations policy questions, starting with how the government has supported stronger engagement with First Nations Australians across agriculture, fisheries and forestry. Can you update the committee on the work?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Absolutely. Our starting point would be the work the department has done on the National Statement on First Nations in Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry. This was a piece of work that was pursued through the agriculture ministers meeting. It was signed by agriculture ministers across Australia, a national piece of work, not just a Commonwealth piece of work. I'll pass to colleagues to talk more about that work, where it's up to and how it's progressing.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: As Mr Lowe said, the national statement was published on 14 August, and it was endorsed by agriculture ministers. It provides a shared policy position for governments to support greater First Nations participation in agriculture, fisheries and forestry. It recognises the significant and continuing contribution by First Nations people to the sectors. It has six priority areas to address barriers and enable opportunities: leadership and workforce, finance and business support, knowledge sharing and safeguards, the Indigenous estate, trade and market access, and government coordination. It has a framework to coordinate effort, share approaches and identify opportunities. It aims to strengthen First Nations economic participation and self-determination.

text: Thank you. I might leave the First Nations and rangers questions till later and go to market access. I've heard that our agricultural trade is more diversified than it has ever been. What is the government doing to support the agriculture sector with trade diversification and expansion?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
The department does focus particularly on new market access, particularly also on maintaining current market access. Where we happen to lose market access, we work very hard to restore that. The department in 2025-26 achieved 56 technical market access outcomes, including five actions to maintain and two actions to restore existing markets, 11 new markets and 38 improvements to existing markets. The committee has heard us talk about new access like Australian blueberries to Vietnam after four years of technical negotiations, with that trade commencing in December 2025. After a significant amount of work we saw the reopening of access to Indonesia for Australian rendered products for animal feed, which had been closed since 2018—so a significant outcome there. Recently, during the visit of the Vietnamese General Secretary and President Tu Lam to Australia, Vietnam agreed to reinstate market access for Australian kangaroo and deer meat, with trade to commence as soon as possible in 2026. That was a recent announcement, in August this year.

The department continues to work very actively across all of our markets and all of our industries, particularly in important markets, improving and safeguarding access for things like halal red meat to Malaysia and finalising the Australia-Malaysia Strategic Halal Red Meat Partnership MOU, which was announced in April, and with a market valued at over $447 million in the 2024-25 financial year. We continue to work across certification of things like pet food to Singapore, feather meal to Taiwan, bovine pericardium tissue to Mexico and the listing of five new beef establishments for export to Indonesia, including one establishment also receiving approval for sheep meat and goat meat, which is the second positive outcome of Indonesian audits of Australian export meat establishments in two years, with a total of seven establishments approved since November.

I have more, Senator, but that goes to the ongoing effort of the department both here in Australia and through our counsellors overseas working very hard with our trading partners to make sure we are maintaining the market that we have and, where possible, expanding that market. We do that, and we have formalised structures to engage with our industries on what their priorities are. We seek to prioritise those as we negotiate with our international markets to make sure that we're extending, maintaining and supporting our exporters.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Senator Tyrrell has some questions.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: On food security, could you explain why it's important for Australia to look simply beyond how much food we produce and consider the broader systems and supply chains that allow food to get from the farm to Australian families?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
As we've been discussing in the committee previously—and I think it is a really important topic to keep discussing with the Senate—it is important that we take a broad view of food security. Some of the lenses that have come up through consultation, through our own analysis and through engagement across government have been ensuring and supporting the productive base of food production in Australia. Obviously, the agricultural production system is vitally important and it is a foundation of our food security in Australia. The resilience of our supply chains is a really important lens in relation to food security—their resilience in terms of not only long-term pressures but also short-term shocks and disruptions. The Middle East is a very good example of that. That's not the only shock. We have talked in this committee previously about H5 as well. Biosecurity shocks, in general, are really important for us to consider in thinking about the resilience of our supply chains and our production systems.

We're concerned with regional economies, which are where so much agricultural production and food processing occurs in Australia, and the vitality of those going forward. We're concerned with the affordability, safety of food and the ability for Australians to access that food, and to ensure that it's nutritious and healthy for them as well. They're some of the domains that we're looking at across the food security strategy.

One of the other observations that this committee was able to reveal is that the nature of food, food policy and the food system is quite disaggregated. There are a number of government agencies that are involved in it. Also, across the economy there are a number of participants in food and, therefore, food security.

What we're concerned with, in relation to thinking about the strategy, and as we develop it, is thinking about it as a system as a whole, and how it works as a system as a whole. How can we think about that in a way that builds Australia's food security as well?
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Would that be considered to be what some of the pressures on the industry are, and how you're trying to manage those and provide solutions?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: From our perspective, it's important to acknowledge some of those pressures and think about the role that a food security strategy can play. We want to be very mindful of any interventions that we might propose or recommend as part of that strategy, so that they are targeted principally to areas which can have maximum impact in relation to supporting Australia's food security going forward. Some of those long-term pressures that you mentioned areas where long-run existing programs support the productivity of Australia's agriculture sector, which is one of the primary drivers of our ability to remain competitive internationally and produce food that's cost-effective and resilient to the shocks that occur, such as drought.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: To pick up on what Mr Lowe was saying, I guess we're using a broad conceptualisation of what food security is. It has to be more than just the amount of food we produce. It's looking at whether people can afford it; whether it's safe and nutritious; whether it can continue to be reliable during shocks; whether people have a say in their choices about the type of food they eat; and whether it's sustainable economically, socially and environmentally. They're the broad dimensions that we're looking at for food security for Australia. It's a big, complex system with multiple component parts.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Which you've highlighted, especially with the international change that we've had. text: Yes, absolutely. If farmers don't have access to them, it becomes quite challenging for them to manage their farming systems. agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: How are the lessons from recent disruptions informing the government's longer-term work on food security?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Two classic examples are the H5 and the Middle East crisis. We have taken them as working examples for the food security strategy. On the Middle East, for example, one of the things that the government thought was important was the establishment of the Fuel and Fertiliser Security Facility. We've talked about that in the committee before. Another one is access to information: how you can give the agriculture sector, in this instance, confidence about what's available and what might be coming up. The creation of our fertiliser dashboard in that instance was important. Also, the government's ability to provide greater information about the fuel supplies that were onshore and what supplies were coming gave the sector greater confidence that they would be able to access fuel and then complete the planting and sowing activities and ultimately—in the current window—harvest activities.

Plastics was one that we worked on with the Department of Industry, Science and Resources to understand exactly how that could impact food security. text: Mr Lowe, can I jump in on that? What I'm hearing on the ground is that there's been, as you say, a perfect storm, in fact. The closure of the wool store has had a terrible impact on wool production in Western Australia. At the same time as the removal of the live export portion of the sheep production decision-making, it means we're seeing less sheep go through abattoirs in Western Australia. We're seeing flock numbers fall. With the wool store, the government was warned that this would absolutely devastate productivity for sheep producers, if you have an attack on both wool and numbers for processing. If you're being told that it's all tickety-boo in Western Australia, that's not the case. The National Party warned, over and over, that this would be the consequence of the shut-down of the live sheep trade in Western Australia. Unfortunately, at each point this has been borne out. I take it the government have a different view, that farmers don't deserve support, but they are happy to support other industries. I want to move on to Russian timber. agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Thanks, Senator. Can I ask for the volume to turned up for our witnesses, please? I don't know if it's just me, but I just struggle to hear. Thank you.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
Yes, as you've said, the team went across to the Philippines to look at banana production practices in the Philippines as part of undertaking our risk assessment. When we were in-country, we did see a range of production practices that the Philippines used that was useful context for us in understanding how the biosecurity risk can potentially be managed. As I think we've discussed previously, what the Philippines have asked us to do is come and assess their existing production practices and then discuss with them whether there are alternative measures that can be applied to the risks of some of those pests that you've mentioned that mean that we could agree to alternatives to those measures that were stipulated under the 2008 biosecurity risk assessment.

We did see evidence of a range of pests and diseases in the banana plantations in the Philippines. That was not unexpected. We anticipated that we would. We saw their management practices, so the particular disease they might be managing would determine the various practices that they implement, including fungicide treatments, bagging of developing bunches of bananas and the like. Certainly, the presence of disease doesn't necessarily mean the risk can't be managed. We need to understand what the risk of transmission of those diseases to Australia through fruit might be and whether they can be managed. To your question about whether it will be published, we have already published a summary of the findings that our technical experts saw in that visit, and that is already publicly available on our website. Certainly, the information that the team has gathered through that process is being used as the team is currently drafting our draft risk assessment report.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: What were the answers to the questions on notice on ABARES's modelling and the northern farms that were visited?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: What we've commissioned ABARES to do is help us with, essentially, one part of the work that we do when we undertake a risk assessment. As I'm sure you would appreciate, the overall risk is a combination of both the likelihood of something occurring and also the consequences of that occurrence happening, should it happen. What we've asked ABARES to do, in particular, is to help us understand the particular impacts on the domestic industry of the introduction of one or any of the pests that we're particularly concerned about. It's a particular economic analysis to make sure that, as we are doing both our likelihood and our consequence assessment, that is informed by an accurate understanding of what the likely consequences, in an economic sense, would be of a pest or disease entering into Australia. That work is well underway. We're expecting that before the end of this calendar year. That will be a key component of the risk analysis work, and we will include that ABARES analysis as an appendix, if you like, to the actual report that we publish.

text: Correct. The analysis is to give us a full picture of the potential impacts on banana growing across Australia. Obviously, a lot of that is concentrated in Queensland but, as you say, there is also New South Wales and even across in Carnarvon.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Exactly. Thank you for reminding me about Carnarvon. I've been pinged about not mentioning Carnarvon more often. Has the department assessed whether the Philippine registration system meets Australian conditions?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Not specifically at this point in time, Senator. That would be, essentially, part of a next phase, if we were to get there. What we're doing right now is trying to work out and complete that assessment of the biosecurity risk, and work out whether there are there measures if a particular risk exceeds our appropriate level of protection, so it's greater than a very low level of risk. For example, if we deem the risk of a particular pest to be high, are there measures that we can put in place to reduce that risk to an acceptable level? If we determine that there are measures, the next phase, before any trade could commence, would be a conversation with the Filipino authorities saying, 'You need to implement these measures to reduce this risk. How are you going to demonstrate to us and give us the assurance that we need that you actually can implement those measures and that those measures will work effectively?' Part of that might be, as you suggest, a look at how the Philippines might register production properties and whether or not their current regime would meet our requirements. That's a next step. If we get to a point where we say, 'Yes, we believe we can reduce the risk to an acceptable level and allow trade to occur safely,' then we need to discuss how they would implement that in practice, in particular to give us the assurance that the measures will do what we expect them to do.

text: You can understand that growers feel that them sharing the cost of dealing with disease following a decision by government to import a product, and potentially a disease, doesn't seem very fair, does it?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Has the government assessed the potential consequences for regional jobs if imported bananas enter the Australian market through that ABARES work?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We are required to focus specifically on the biosecurity risk. As part of assessing biosecurity risk, what we cannot take account of is what the economic consequences of increased competition, for example, might be. Neither can we take into account the potential benefits to the Australian economy if we were to enable imports from a particular country. So the benefits or disbenefits, from that point of view, are not something that we can consider in our biosecurity risk assessment. However, what we absolutely can do, and is central to what we do—and this is why we've commissioned the work from ABARES—is seek to understand the economic consequences of an incursion of any of the pests that we're assessing, and so it's that element of it that is a very strong focus of our assessment.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: So jobs will be part of that economic assessment?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: From the point of view of understanding the impacts of an incursion, for example, of moko into Far North Queensland, that would have, no doubt, an impact on the local economies, and potentially jobs in that context, certainly yes, but from the point of view of enabling imports, and let's say they've got great measures and we never have a disease incursion, we cannot take account of the benefit or disbenefit of the trade in bananas as such.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: So who would look at the economic analysis of the benefit of having a strong banana industry in Australia and, of course, the secondary part, the food security element, should we have supply routes impacted? We've shut down or abolished most of the banana growers in Australia, should there be highly competitive, cheaper imports. We then aren't able to access bananas because of a supply chain disruption. Does anybody assess the potential impacts on food security in Australia?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I would suggest that some of those things could appropriately be considered through the food security strategy. I guess, more broadly, from a trade point of view, as I think we've discussed today already, Australia is an exporter of agricultural produce, so part of engaging in this process where we undertake risk assessments to consider the market access requests from our trading partners is part of us also then expecting, and getting, good buy-in from our trading partners in them assessing our agricultural commodities for export. It's part of our broader approach to trade, and the fact that we are reliant on having good access to multiple markets around the world to be able to sell our agricultural produce, and part of that equation is that we also need to engage with things like this risk assessment, and then, undertaking the risk assessment, we set our own appropriate level of protection. If, at the end of that risk assessment, we conclude that it can't be done safely, then that's the answer, but we have engaged with the WTO expectations and commitments that we've made as a signatory to the sanitary and phytosanitary agreement and the benefits that then accrue to Australia for engaging with that and us being seen as a reliable and safe trading partner.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I appreciate that free trade element but, as a small population that's geographically isolated from other parts of the world, there is a risk that it's not only the jobs and the industry and the expertise, but also what happens if supply chains are significantly cut and we actually find ourselves without bananas.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Absolutely, Senator. I hear you, and, as I say, I think there are other avenues for exploring some of those issues. When it comes to the biosecurity risk assessment, I have to focus specifically on that biosecurity scope.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: So, on the food security element—

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: The food security strategy is being developed, and was discussed under outcome 1, Senator. The sorts of things that we'll consider are the production of all food in the country and what are the dependencies and vulnerabilities, I guess, in that. Obviously, we're looking at it at a relatively high level, but the fact that we're reliant on imports for a particular thing, for example, or that we want something onshore and available to us, would both be relevant factors in considering the food security strategy.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

text: What Commonwealth funding is currently available for H5 preparedness and response in 2026-27. As we're here today, how much funding is available?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Thank you for your question. The Australian government has committed more than $270 million to strengthen H5 bird flu surveillance, preparedness and response capability. That includes more than $13 million committed since 2024 to strengthen surveillance, preparedness and response capability across the agriculture, environment and health portfolios, and $13.4 million in Commonwealth contributions to cost-share national H5 bird flu response activities under the Emergency Animal Disease Response Agreement, approved by the National Management Group in July 2026. There has been a small increase to that in recent days. I stand to be corrected, but I think it's about an additional $4 million. We also have $125 million announced in August 2026 to support immediate national emergency biosecurity response activities for H5 bird flu, which are cost-shared equally by the Commonwealth, states and territories. That includes $15 million in Commonwealth contributions to cost-share national H5 bird flu response activities under the National Management Agreement for H5 in wildlife. There is the EADRA, which is the response that we deal with in regard to agriculture in particular. Then, of course, we have the new arrangement we entered into to deal with H5, which specifically relates to the wildlife aspects. Finally, we have $20 million, announced in August 2026, to boost and extend on-ground action for key native wildlife species and locations, and emergency response activities for native wildlife, including Commonwealth-managed national parks and supporting citizen science work.

text: There hasn't been specific modelling that I'm aware of about the veterinary workforce. However, we do have a very well established emergency response arrangement within Australia. There are veterinarians employed with state departments who are responsible for managing the outbreak. For example, in the H7 outbreak, there were veterinarians alongside other professionals involved in managing the outbreak in poultry for H7 in 2024 and 2025. Those veterinarians undertake a range of functions within those response structures, and that's all managed under those existing arrangements. There are also mechanisms in place for private veterinarians to be engaged by those response jurisdictions, should they have a need to, and there are some standardised guidelines about how that would occur. agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Alright. Is there anything you can add?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
Yes, only that veterinary workforce shortages have been recognised as a longstanding issue. Of course, it's not an issue that affects just government services or this type of response. The majority of veterinarians work in private practice, and we know that there's also a maldistribution element to the veterinary workforce, particularly in rural and regional areas. We do engage regularly with the Australian Veterinary Association and the Australasian Veterinary Board Council. We've had longstanding engagements with them to understand the issue and to work with them on what policy levers, if you like, or actions, could help to alleviate the veterinary workforce shortage. It's also not unique to Australia. I would say that there is a global veterinary workforce issue, with many of the partner countries that we work with, particularly through our Quad alliance with Canada, the United States, New Zealand and the United Kingdom. We're also sharing lessons with them.

In Australia, since 2024, my office has been involved in trying to bring together the relevant stakeholders. Obviously, it's a complex, multifactorial issue and it needs to be resolved throughout the profession. We have convened two roundtable discussions so that we can understand what's needed. We have funded an independent taskforce to help us to design for the information needs there are, to help inform the policy choices. Some of those policy choices sit within other departments, including, for example, the Department of Education. As a result of that, we have agreed that the department will initially lead a snapshot of veterinary workforce data. The main feedback we get, when we're talking about the options to help alleviate some of these issues, is the lack of available data to inform those policy decisions, so it is the first step that we need to undertake. We have committed to the Commonwealth, through my office, to leading that work, with the aim of delivering a first national veterinary data snapshot by July 2027. We're just progressing that now, after the Agriculture Senior Officials Committee has agreed to us doing that, and we'll be looking to engage more broadly on a sustainable approach to doing that so that we have longitudinal data.

text: Excellent. As I understand it, on notice, you've said the current policy is to eradicate H5 in poultry without vaccination. Is that correct?

text: I further understand that the vaccination policy is under review, in conjunction with the states and territories. Is that correct?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: With the states and territories and industry. I'll just clarify that the policy itself is to eradicate without the use of vaccination. Globally, due to the sustained impacts of H5 in the poultry industries, the attitudes towards vaccination and the practices are changing and we're very aware of and monitoring those. What we're doing is developing the policy frameworks that we would apply if we make a decision to apply vaccination in the future. The intent is not to decide whether we vaccinate now or not. It's to make sure that, if we need to move to vaccination, we know how we're going to do it, because there are quite a number of complexities associated with that decision. That work is being undertaken jointly with the states and territories and also the peak industry bodies.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Following questions from my colleagues Senator Scarr and Senator Bleyer, these dollar figures seem strikingly small for such a huge continent, with so much at stake. Are you confident that enough is being spent on bird flu?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Absolutely, Senator. We're very well prepared and we have a very comprehensive surveillance program. It's actually a conversation Dr Cookson and I have had, because, to be honest, we all prepared for the worst-case scenario and, from the modelling we're doing and the international experience, we had expected it would be worse than it has been. We've been, to be frank, pleasantly surprised that it hasn't. Dr Cookson can talk more technically about some of theories about why this is so. New Zealand is in the same position, as you might know—very small numbers of detections, and they thought, during the spring, they would see more. agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I wanted to ask about these confirmed events. I'm very concerned that you don't have the data on the numbers of birds and mammals that are dying. It seems to me that just reporting an event doesn't really give us a handle on what's happening on the ground. One crested tern dying compared to, potentially, hundreds of penguins—those are two very different events, and yet all we know is that there are 723 confirmed events, with 53 in Tassie. Why don't we have that data yet? Surely that is critical to understanding the extent of bird flu in Australia.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Our focus has been on actually monitoring the trends—looking at the national implications, and, certainly from an agriculture perspective, being very conscious of watching the movements of this virus so that we can ensure that we are adequately prepared for any potential spillover in industries. That's a key priority, and the data assists us in that regard in terms of managing and monitoring that risk. Dr Cookson can probably talk further on this, but a lot of the data you're referring to is held by jurisdictions. We just don't capture it on the national dashboard, and I think there's some variation in terms of what's recorded state by state—certainly the more granular information is held at that level.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Biosecurity, Operations and Compliance Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: How is the extent not linked to the number of birds or mammals that are dying in an event? Again, you could have thousands of birds found dead, and on your database it's one event.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
As I said previously, the national dashboard is a public information tool. It's there to inform the public about where H5 bird flu has been detected and, indeed, where it has not. I think it's really important to put into perspective that, of the investigations that are occurring every day across the country, there have now been more than 4,915 negative investigations over the time. One of the considerations is how you reliably determine what's died from H5 and what's died from another cause. We've always had underlying mortality in our wildlife across Australia and we certainly can't assume that every dead animal has died from H5.

On saying that, we do really acknowledge the concerns around impact evaluations, and that is going to be important for long-term population monitoring. It is a cross-sectoral response, so, while we deal with the biosecurity side of it, we're working very closely with our colleagues in environment departments and also engage regularly with non-government organisations involved in biodiversity and conservation. We are taking advice from them on what the needs are. We are working, still, on what reporting will be required into the future. We've certainly had some initial discussions about what impact monitoring can be done. Some of the jurisdictions have indicated that they're already doing some things. There will be sites and there will be species that have been under population monitoring. It's about building on those existing mechanisms to make sure that the data is available over time to understand what the resilience needs are of some of those wild populations, but a lot of that information and advice is coming through environment and conservation departments.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: When will we have that data? On the basis of what you've just said, we, as senators, could be looking at this information and we could think 723 birds have died, but it could be 723 million birds. How is it acceptable that you don't have that information? Do you have that information and you're not publishing it, or is it that you simply don't have the data to make that analysis?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I don't have that information, as I explained.

Someone has this data. Why haven't you even requested it from the states and territories?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think that we would need a purpose to do that. I think the point that Ms Saunders was trying to make earlier is that there may well be a lot more data held at state and territory level, but, from a national perspective, we're looking at how we guide the response, where the risks are to industry, in terms of the further spread of the disease. I appreciate that there's a lot of interest in individual data but, for us, what we need to see, as Ms Saunders has said, is the trends, what risk we need to manage, and working with states and territories for that. We are looking at this outbreak as a whole. Population-level data is not something that helps the department of agriculture right now to understand the dynamics of this disease outbreak—and we really have to prioritise that, to be honest. That is our job: to understand how this disease is moving through populations and to prepare for what might be coming next. Again, I appreciate that it may be of interest to a range of other stakeholders, and it is of interest to us, but, in the context of managing a national disease outbreak, we really have to be careful about where we focus our effort, and counting birds, to be honest, is not really going to help us manage the disease outbreak at this point.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Just on the counting bit, one of the concerns that's been raised with me by people on the ground is around this mass mortality event. We know that in Australia we're really bad at funding environmental monitoring. We have some of the most amazing scientists, but we just haven't put sustained effort in. We're essentially data-deficient for a whole range of these species. I'm hearing from people who are saying, 'We're having hundreds of birds die,' and are being told, 'We've got no baseline data on that population, so it's not a mass mortality event.' agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: As we've indicated—my position hasn't changed—we are interested in trends as they relate to this disease and its movement around the country, so that we can manage those risks, particularly as it relates to spillover into agriculture. Certainly, that's our department's role. Yes, we have a broader coordination arrangement as it relates to the impacts of H5 with wildlife, and we took on that leadership role because we have the governance arrangements and we have the operational capability to support Environment in its efforts in terms of managing those risks as they relate to environment. agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Maybe just finally, what does success look like in combating bird flu in Australia?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: It's minimising the risk as best we can, both in wildlife and in agriculture industry. That's what success is. It's gone incredibly well so far, in that we haven't seen a spillover to industry, but our efforts are all around working with industry to ensure that we minimise the impacts for when and if that occurs. That's our priority now.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Biosecurity, Operations and Compliance Group

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Could I just add that the international experience has been that broadscale impacts in wildlife populations, once it's present and circulating as it is in Australia, are very hard to minimise, and that's why the focus has been to mitigate the worst impacts where possible. The preparedness that has been undertaken over the last two years has focused on areas where resilience and population-level support can be provided for the most vulnerable species. I can't speak in detail to that. That has been led through our Threatened Species Commissioner and DCCEEW, as well as our state environmental agencies, but certainly, while we focus on preparing the agricultural industry for potential outbreaks, there has been an equal focus on where those priority species are and what resilience to build healthy populations that can bounce back can be, and what actions can be taken to protect the most vulnerable, and that has included things like investing in the evidence base to ensure that vaccines, for example, can be applied safely as part of that. It's certainly been recognising the role that enhanced biosecurity at those facilities that house important breeding populations from conservation has as well. A range of actions have already been taken to, as best as possible, support resilient populations, and that's the best approach that's been taken globally.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Okay. Could I give some context, because I do think context is important, before I go specifically to your question. What we have is an integrated early detection surveillance network, which is supported by the Commonwealth, states and territories and domestic industries, so there's a shared responsibility, as is the case for biosecurity more generally. In this instance, what we saw was, firstly, that no biosecurity system can eliminate all risk. We know that, but we do manage it, and you've heard earlier evidence from my colleagues about appropriate levels of protection. Australia's system uses multiple layers of protection to achieve that, and that's designed to detect pests as early as possible, so pre-border where we can, and at border, and then we ensure we have a rapid response where we do see incursions post-border. That is really important, and it's a layered response. Success isn't purely through surveillance or the identification of a nest through a lure, for example. It is multi-layered throughout. In this case, routine surveillance, undertaken by our department, detected the ants before any evidence of wider establishment was identified. This is successful, and we should have great confidence in relation to the work we do across the continuum, because what we have is surveillance findings, through to treatment controls, training, and the work with industries and states and territories. We've identified it very early, and responded quickly.

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Biosecurity, Operations and Compliance Group

text: The decision about public communication was a matter for New South Wales. However, I guess what's important here is, first, you need to make sure that, when communicating with the public, we know exactly what we're communicating, what we're saying the nature of the risk is, and what we need them to do. Until that initial response was underway, you run the risk of going out too early and alarming unnecessarily and/or giving factually incorrect information to the public and not being clear on what we need of them. An appropriate period of time was taken to, firstly, respond; it wasn't as though agencies just sat and waited for this work to be done. A whole range of activities were undertaken as soon as the risk was identified, including surveillance. I talked about the tracing of containers, surveillance, the inclusion of detector dogs to understand the nature of the risk, and, of course, as you touched on, the genetic work that we asked Queensland to do to confirm its source, all of which goes to inform the full extent of the response and how you might engage with the community.

text: You talked about the amount of time and when the surveillance has occurred, but once again it gets back to the context. We talked about integrated approaches, pre- and post-border activities, and there's also a piece about risk. There's been a real focus on the ant biology. That's where you referred to Mr Jack Gough and his reference to six months, for example, because the ant biology would suggest that's when you could see spread. There has been no movement of ants within that area. We have not identified any in that time. I also want to point out, though, that, when we consider risk and the nature of the response and how much surveillance we do, we consider a number of factors. We're informed by the assessment of the goods arriving, combined with the volume of goods, relevant intelligence, such as the country of origin, and compliance history. There's a range of factors we consider, and noting that we're also managing hundreds of biosecurity risks. Red imported fire ants, we know, are a significant risk. You see the investment we're making in South-East Queensland, where we're absolutely committed to eradicating it. We know this is an important risk, but it's one of many that we're managing. We've also engaged the Inspector-General of Biosecurity, who is already embarking, in agreement with us, on looking at the way we manage risk across the continuum, and her immediate priority is to look at this as a case study to see how effective our measures are, and if they need to change.

text: Okay, thanks, Chair. Thank you for appearing tonight. Fire ants continue to spread throughout Queensland, despite information put out by the Fire Ant Eradication Program to the contrary. text: What quarantine procedures and border protection strategies are being considered to manage future intrusions?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: As per my earlier evidence, we have a layered approach to managing biosecurity, pre, at and post border. We have agreements with offshore countries, we have fumigation arrangements with jurisdictions, depending on the nature of the goods coming across the border, we have assurance and we have surveillance activities pre-border, at the border and then, of course, post-border. We don't say that we can prevent every risk coming across the border; we cannot. That's an impossible task, but we do manage, and have very successfully managed, the risk to appropriate level of protection, which is close to zero but not zero. We've done that very well. When it occurs post border, we work collectively with jurisdictions and other stakeholders and industry in managing those risks.

text: There have been a few questions taken on notice there. I might just ask a couple of quick questions about pineapples. Can I get an update on the status of the risk assessment on the proposed importation of pineapples from India and Indonesia.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
We've released a draft risk assessment for the risks in relation to the importation of decrowned pineapples from both India and Indonesia. That went out for public consultation on 16 July. We received some requests from stakeholders to extend that, so we did extend that period, which closed on 5 October, a couple of weeks ago now. We are currently engaged in reviewing all of that feedback that we have received from those stakeholders, and, as we work through that, any influence that has on the outcomes of the risk assessment we will document and provide back as we work through that process.

One thing to clarify is that this is not a new pathway, as such, for decrowned pineapples. We do already have conditions for the importation of decrowned pineapples from the Philippines, Solomon Islands, Thailand, Sri Lanka and Taiwan. So this assessment is essentially to look and see, for pineapples sourced from India and Indonesia, whether there are any particular differences in the risk that they might pose that might mean they can't safely be imported into Australia and/or whether or not different measures would need to apply.
witness_organisation: Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Is that the reason the government is not doing a full biosecurity import risk analysis?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: Essentially, yes. When we undertake a BIRA, or when we undertake any risk assessment, we would do an analysis to work out what is the most appropriate mechanism to undertake that risk analysis. Generally, some of the guidelines for when we would undertake a biosecurity import risk analysis, the regulated process, are if it's a completely new pathway or if we believe there might be quite significance differences in the biosecurity risk that the new proposed importation would suggest. In this particular case it didn't meet that threshold. But certainly what I can commit to is that, as we work through the process of developing the final report and considering all the stakeholder feedback, we will engage the members of the scientific advisory group in their capacity as independent experts to provide a view on our risk assessment work and also a view on whether or not they feel we have appropriately considered stakeholder feedback.
