We are aware of additional views, particularly around some bacterial rot pathogens—about whether or not strains that are present in other parts of the world may be different to the strains that are present here in Australia, and we will give that information very careful consideration.

text: My understanding is you proposed taking a systems approach with regard to India and Indonesia. How is that going to be verified and audited?

text: Our approach is to work through the risks and determine whether or not there are appropriate measures that can mitigate the risk to our appropriate level of protection. The other element to that is ourselves thinking about and working through what additional assurance and verification framework we would need to put over the top of that to be confident that the measures as imagined are the measures in practice. text: I have some questions about pomelos. Is that the right pronunciation? It's not something I'm all that familiar with. agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text:
Certainly. We established a pathway for the importation of pomelos from Vietnam. I'm sorry, just bear with me so that I can make sure I get the right dates. If I go slightly wrong, I'll correct it. After we completed a risk assessment, we worked through a conversation with our Vietnamese counterparts to develop what we call the operational work plan, which turns the risk assessment into practical things that the trading partner needs to do to meet our requirements, and so trade then commenced. As the trade began, we started to observe pests and diseases on the pathway that we didn't expect should be there. As you said, one of the main mechanisms for managing particular pests that could be on the pathway was a systems approach, and a well-implemented system that's working at the level we would expect should mean that fruit that is arriving in Australia is in very good condition and there's no evidence of pests or diseases of any type, let alone pests and diseases with a specific biosecurity risk.

As we started to observe that—obviously, each consignment was managed on its merits at the time, so, as required, additional testing may have been done to determine what the pests were and what risks they presented—we continued to see consignments that were not giving us confidence the system was working as expected. We brought up the date on which we had some of our officials go across and do an in-country audit. Whenever we establish a new trade, it's our general practice that, within that first 12 months of trade, we will get some of our very experienced auditors across to our trading partner to make sure that the pathway has been established in a way that's consistent with what we had agreed with our trading partner. We began to be concerned that that may not have been occurring, so we sent our auditors across.

As a result of that audit, their findings indicated, consistent with what we'd been seeing at the border, that the system that should be implemented was not being implemented in the way that was meeting our requirements and managing the risk to an appropriate level. As a consequence of that, following some risk assessment work that we did, the secretary in her capacity as the director of biosecurity issued a suspended goods determination on 15 September 2026 to suspend that trade from Vietnam.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

In some cases, there were partial disruptions of consignments; in some cases, entire consignments were rejected—and it was based on biosecurity assessment of individual consignments at that point in time. However, from my perspective, sitting back and looking at what was going on, I became concerned that, overall, the pathway was not performing to an acceptable level, which is why we did the work and asked the director of biosecurity to act.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: We have completed an audit report, which we've now provided back to Vietnam. The systems approach has measures in place right across the production chain, from things that need to occur in the orchard through to things that need to occur at picking in the packhouse and things that the Vietnamese competent authority needs to do, as far as their own inspection, audit and assurance. Essentially, we had concerns across nearly all of those elements, so we have provided very clear information back to the Vietnamese about what those concerns have been. That's with them now. We will continue to work with them, but we are waiting for them to provide us with their response to our findings and also what it is they would propose that they believe can address those findings. It's only if we come to the view that they have appropriately addressed our concerns and that the measures that they have put in place will reduce the risk to an acceptable level that we would contemplate recommencing trade.

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: This systems based approach sounds to me like it's only as strong as every link in the chain. Are there any lessons here for this approach, particularly going back to the issues of bananas and pineapples, given this has failed very early on?

agency: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
text: I think there are a range of lessons here. It's also something that is increasingly becoming something that we are relying on for our own exports, but equally that many of our trading partners are asking us to consider for imports to Australia. As a result, the IPPC—International Plant Protection Convention—who is the standard-setting body, continues to do work on international standards in relation to systems approaches. The CSIRO has been doing a lot of work in relation to systems approaches and how they work effectively. So, certainly for us, we will be continuing to monitor and think very carefully about systems approaches—and, in particular, from my perspective, the key element is the assurance and verification. How can we be sure that what our trading partner says the system is doing is actually doing, and how do we get appropriate verification of that?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: We now welcome Dr Ashley Bunce. Thanks for coming along, Dr Bunce. In the interests of time, would you like to make a brief opening statement?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Thank you very much. Senator Bleyer.

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: It's really good to see this role finally filled. What have you been up to since you started in the role?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text:
Thank you. I started in the role on 1 May this year, so I'm coming up to almost six months in the role. In the time that I've been in the role, I've been doing various things. At the last estimates, I commented I had been doing a lot of stakeholder engagement. I felt it was important as a new inspector-general to go, particularly given the length of time between when my predecessor left the role, and re-engage with stakeholders, so I've done a lot of trips to Darwin, Perth, Portland and now Townsville more recently, to go and meet with industry and go and observe what happens in the live export trade. I've been to what they call registered establishments and seen vets going through and doing inspections. I've spoken to the vets. I've spoken to the operators and spoken to industry. I've also met with a lot of animal welfare groups as well. I've met with the key animal welfare groups in that time, and it has been really important for me to hear the perspectives of all those different groups, around the live animal export trade, to help inform the work programs that I've been developing.

In terms of the things I've been focused on, the first thing was to publish an annual work plan. One of the requirements for the inspector-general is to publish an annual work plan. I published a work plan on 6 August, I believe it was, this year. That's been published. It outlines the reviews that I'm intending to do this year. One of the things coming into the role—my predecessor had commenced two reviews, but they were essentially unfinished at the time that she left the role. I've inherited those reviews and I've been working on those, one of those reviews in particular.

I've also published the annual report, which I believe went up last week on the website. Again, one of the requirements of the role is to publish an annual report each year which outlines the activities that have been performed by the office in that previous year. I'm also happy to announce that I've developed a memorandum of understanding with the department which has been signed off today. So that has been a great achievement as well.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Today?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Today. It got signed today, so—
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: [Inaudible].

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Not quite. It actually came through this afternoon, and I was just getting ready and I thought, 'Yep, we'll sign that and get that moving.' So that has been signed as well. I am in the process, as I indicated, of one of those reviews that was started by Dr Katherine Clift. I provided it to the department for a fact-check—I believe it was 25 September. They responded, I believe, on 16 October, and my office and I are going through, looking at the responses to that process and considering any changes or amendments to the report before we finalise it.

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Is that someone from the department, or do you second people from the department?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: It's from the department. The department allocate staff to the office to support the functions of the role, and there's one staff member who's allocated to essentially manage the operations of the office.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Do you also still hold the position as ACT commissioner for sustainability and the environment?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: I do, yes. They're both part-time roles. In addition to inspector-general, which is a part-time role, I'm also a part-time commissioner with the ACT government as Commissioner for Sustainability and the Environment.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: And do you split the roles on an as needs basis or you clearly define what you do each day of the week?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Yes, they are clearly defined. The commissioner role is more of a what would you call a normal part-time role—there are a number of days per week that I work in that role. With the inspector-general role there's a cap of up to 120 days per year under the Remuneration Tribunal, and so that is then flexible based on the work program that I do as the inspector-general. At this stage I've committed to the department that I'll do the inspector-general role on a Friday, but then other days as required. For instance, if there are travels required or there are other things that are required, then I'll do additional days on a needs basis.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Given your role is to independently assess the department, do you find that there are challenges involved in that independence when your staff is from the department?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: I haven't found that to date. The staff that have been allocated—so when I started the role, a staff member retired at the end of the June, and the new staff member actually used to work for the Inspector-General of Biosecurity and has worked, I believe, for all the inspector-generals of biosecurity. So he's well understanding of what the role is and the separation between my role and the department. The MOU deals with a lot of those arrangements and puts in place just trying to protect that independence.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: You already touched on this in your very helpful answer to my first question around what you've gotten up to, but, just to recap and ask you some questions about it, in August 2024, the then inspector-general published a report on the department's performance in implementing the I-G's recommendations from six prior reports published between March 2020 and April 2024.

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: You're obviously aware of that. You've caught up very well, I can tell. That report found that, out of 48 recommendations, the department had only implemented 13 as at August 2024, but the then inspector-general disputed that number and said the actual number was six. In the latest annual report, the department now claims to have closed 27 of the 48 recommendations. Have I got it right so far?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: There has been an update since that annual report.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: I look forward to hearing from you about that, because that would leave 21 open. But closing doesn't necessarily mean that implementation is complete. Do you agree with that?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text:
I would, yes. Part of the role is—just to go back, sorry. Of the 48 recommendations, our department has now closed 32 of those recommendations, and there are 16 that remain open. The department has a process for reviewing the implementation of recommendations, and there's a determination by the department on whether those actions have been completed and can be closed or if they remain open. That's separate to my role, but, obviously, one of the functions of this role is to look at—in any independent oversight body, we need to consider how effective we are in our role, and part of that is making sure that those recommendations are implemented to full effect, given the nature of what the intention of the recommendations was.

I think it's important to periodically go back and look at previous reviews and recommendations and, in particular, the department's decision to close recommendations and to independently assess whether that meets the intent of what the recommendation was. I have met with Mr Ross Carter. He was the first inspector-general. I've also had a number of meetings with Dr Katherine Clift as well, and I've spoken to them about their reviews and their recommendations. I have those relationships so that, if at some point in the future I determine that it will be useful to go back and look at reviews and implementation recommendations, I'm able to go. One of the things is, when you draft recommendations, as an inspector-general, you have in your mind clear what you want—intent in that. There's an art and a craft to writing recommendations so that it's clear about what the intent and the recommendation is but it provides some flexibility to the department about how it's actually implemented. It's useful to have those relationships to go and test with those people who wrote those recommendations at the time whether it did actually meet what they were intending.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Are you familiar with the recommendation from 2021 for the department to trial the use of body cameras for regional veterinary officers and auditors during inspections and on-site audits? It looks to me like that has been closed but all that occurred was that there was an agreement in principle to the concept. Has there actually been some meaningful attention to that recommendation on the use of body cameras?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: I'm aware at a high level of the previous reviews. I'm not aware of that particular recommendation and what the department has done in relation to that recommendation, but I'm happy to take that on notice and turn my attention to it in the future.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Thank you. Please do formally take that on notice. Have you been able to do an assessment of how many of the 48 recommendations from your predecessors have actually been adequately implemented? I think you gave us an update on the number that you see as having been addressed, but, in your opinion—I can see that you approach this as a genuine professional—what about proper implementation of those 48 recommendations? What do you say?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text:
It's not something I've turned my attention to at this point in time. My focus has been really on trying to progress those two reviews that were undertaken by my predecessor, given there's been a period of time now since they were done and completed. I think it's important. Given the range of work and input provided by a whole range of stakeholders to inform those reviews, I think it's really important and necessary for me to get those published and out in the public domain, so that's been my focus to date: to try and get those reviews progressed.

Part of the consultation I've been doing with stakeholders is hearing from them what they see as their priorities for me to give some attention to and to consider, and there are a range of topics that they've highlighted with me that they see as the highest priorities. The implementation of recommendations has been raised, but it's certainly not up there in the list of priorities that stakeholders have raised with me that they'd like me to give some priority to. I think at some point in time I will look at those implementation recommendations, but, again, with a part-time role with one staff member, I need to focus my energy on where I'm going to get the best outcomes, so that's the approach I'm taking.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: In that regard, what's the most urgent recommendation that the government needs to implement, do you think? What you consider urgent would, I imagine, take your time with priority.

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: I'm probably not able to answer that. Like I said, I've been focused on getting those other reviews completed rather than looking at the implementation of previous recommendations, noting that the last report was done in 2024; we're only about two years out from it now, so it probably will come up at a point in time to look at that again. But my priority has been on the existing reviews and commencing my annual work plan as well.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: The recommendation from 2021 for the department to update the Exporter Supply Chain Assurance System animal welfare standards to be consistent with the World Organisation for Animal Health's terrestrial animal health group remains open. agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: I suggest that's a question for the department. I'm not able to answer that.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: Is it something that you can take on notice or is it outside of your remit?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports
text: What's your role as inspector-general in the phase-out and ending of live sheep export by May 2028?

agency: Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports

My role directly is to provide oversight and assurance that the department is performing its role as a regulator effectively, and part of the reasoning for doing the review around the regulatory framework is it's quite timely, with the phase-out of live sheep, to look at the whole regulatory framework which has been developed over many years in response to various incidents across a whole range of trade and, with the phase-out of live sheep, taking an independent look at that framework and providing advice to the government about any improvements that would be recommended.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: We'll now call the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority. Colleagues, I believe Senator Bleyer has something to with her staff and has requested to kick off. Senator, is that correct? Let me check with my colleagues that that's alright.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Yes. I know I'm a rookie and I'm seeking an indulgence, but I would be grateful if I could have it on this occasion. Thank you, Chair.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Sure. The committee is happy to work with you. I welcome officers from the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority. Mr Hansen, we welcome you. Do you want to make an opening statement?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: No thanks, Chair. I think we're all ready to go.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: We appreciate that; we've got a few people to get through. Senator Bleyer.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: In October 2025, the APVMA issued a trade notice relating to a permit for the use of florfenicol in Tasmania for farmed Atlantic salmon. Of course, you're aware of that. You relied on rainbow trout data from a 2014 study. You had no data on how residues in Atlantic salmon fall away, and you recommended conservative volumes of florfenicol regarding risk of residues, noting the limited dataset and the absence of residues-declined data in the target species—that's Atlantic salmon. Then, in March 2026, you suspended the permit for unacceptable risk of residue exposure to non-target species. You accept all of that?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Why was the risk to wild seafood, such as rock lobster and abalone, not assessed before the permit was issued?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text:
All the international data that we had looked at had indicated that there wasn't a risk of accumulation in wild fishery species. Looking around the globe in terms of where this had been used, there was no—the calculations were about what would be present in the water streams outside of the pens, outside of feeding times. We were comfortable with the presence that was going to be there. We were comfortable with the fact that it was not going to have an acute toxicity or an impact on any of the native species. In fact, we chose an algae which is the most sensitive to florfenicol as our lower limit.

All of the work that has been done around the globe has not demonstrated any accumulation in other wild-caught fisheries that occur around these pens. The detections in abalone and the detections in rock lobsters were unable to be explained in terms of either the method or the mechanism for transfer from the feeding sites to the distances—up to over 11 kilometres away in the end. That was why, in the presence of that information being provided to us by the Tasmanian NRE off the back of their monitoring for those species, we suspended the permit and went back to the applicant to say: 'Something is occurring here which doesn't appear in any of the data that has been provided. You need to explain us why and how.'
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: You said that to NRE?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: No—to the applicant, who was Abbey Laboratories.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: To the applicant.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Yes. They also couldn't explain the how and why, and were therefore unable to mitigate that, so the permit was cancelled.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Did you initially put any reliance on the EPA's results, which were much more kind to the impact of this chemical than—you relied on it then. You won't rely on the EPA's results in future, given they only detected florfenicol 35 metres outside of the fish-farming zone, if I can call it that, whereas the NRE did some subsequent testing and discovered it up to 14 kilometres away, as you said.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Yes. That was the really perplexing part for us. It didn't appear in the water more than 35 metres away from the pens, and yet it was appearing kilometres away. That mechanism for transfer has been one of the bits that obviously either requires an answer to be given about how to mitigate risk for wild-caught species or other plans for how you mitigate that risk need to be developed. Whilst we are comfortable with that emergency use permit, with the impact and the residues in the fish that were being treated with the one treatment of up to 10 days of treatment; while we were comfortable with the environmental dispersion of that one treatment in those pens over that period of time and environmental impact, we obviously—even though those levels that were being detected in the abalone, the rock lobsters and other species were at such miniscule levels that they were just above the quantum of detection, especially for a product that is not registered in other products the quantum of detection means zero tolerance by trading partners, which creates an obvious trade risk for us, and that's one of the key criteria that we assess against.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: The permit that the trade notice related to has been cancelled, but Abbey Laboratories has made another permit application, hasn't it?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: We have a couple of applications in front of us at the moment.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: From Abbey?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: We have one from Abbey Laboratories and one from Salmon Tasmania. Salmon Tasmania has an application in front of us at the moment for an emergency use permit along a similar path as the previous permit; that's in the south-eastern biosecurity zone for the treatment dose rates and frequency of the previous permit. What they have submitted to try to address the trade question, which is obviously still outstanding for us, is the Aquaculture Therapeutant—Wild Fisheries Market Management Plan that the Tasmanian department has developed not just for florfenicol but for any therapeutic uses in the salmon industry about how to minimise or mitigate the risk to trade with regard to wild-caught species. We're currently assessing that.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: You mentioned the general location of Salmon Tasmania's application. Where does Abbey Laboratories' new permit application relate to?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: There's a second application, which is a minor use permit. It's looking to move the location to not just the south-eastern biosecurity zone but the eastern biosecurity zone as well and to increase the dose rates and the treatment regime. That's proposed, and that obviously has a significant amount of work that is being done to look at environmental impacts, to look at any microbial resistance impact as well as residues and depletion.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: It's a much bigger area and a much higher dose, so there's a much higher likelihood of unacceptable risk of residue exposure, including to non-target species. That's right, isn't it?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: That's right. That's what we need to calculate before we can consider whether it gets approved or not.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: When are you intending to decide on those permit applications?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Once we arrive at a conclusion out of the science as to whether—in fact, for both of them, once we arrive at the science in terms of meeting the safety criteria, the efficacy criteria, we will go back out for a trade advisory notice consultation with stakeholders and community to get all of the industries' and the community's views with regard to what's being proposed and what the potential impact on trade would be.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: That's very thorough of you. About 9,000 tonnes of farmed fish died between January and March 2026; you're aware of that? And that was despite the antibiotic; that's right, isn't it?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: I believe so, yes.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Did the permit require data on whether treatment worked?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Yes, and that information needs to be provided to us to support their follow-up application.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: What does it show?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: I'd have to take that on notice. I don't have that in front of me.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: But it's been provided?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: I call on the two permit applications to be produced, and I call on the data that Salmon Tasmania has given you on whether the treatment worked, and there's a date by which that material can be provided. Thank you very much.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: I'll go to Senator Pocock, then I'll go across to Senator Thorpe and, if there are any other questions, I'll go to the deputy chair.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text:
Thank you for your time this evening. Mr Hansen, I want to talk paraquat and, looking at your decision, I want to walk through the APVMA's analysis of the published literature as it relates to paraquat. I want to start with Brent and Schaeffer 2011, and I've got a copy to circulate if it's helpful for people. The APVMA states:

Brent and Schaeffer (2011) examined the entire body of published reports of clinical outcomes of survivors of paraquat poisoning and found no connection between high dose paraquat exposure in humans and the development of Parkinson's disease.

However, what the APVMA failed to state is that Dr Brent, at the time he authored that review, was a consultant to Syngenta, who manufacture paraquat, and they also failed to state that the long-term survivors included any person who lived beyond 30 days after poisoning. Parkinson's has a latency of years to decades, and this study looked at people just 30 days after poisoning. In fact, my team went and found a letter to the editor that Dr Brent had written about his study where he himself acknowledges that no conclusion could be made about chronic low-dose exposure to paraquat and its association with Parkinson's. As a science based agency, what would you say the limitations of this study were? There weren't any mentioned in your regulatory documents.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: While my colleague Mr Deller pulls that individual paper up—as you would be aware, we literally looked at hundreds of studies, and, in our additional neurotoxicity report that we produced to go along with the final regulatory decision, we explained the approach that we took with regard to the weighting of evidence and how we treated and viewed evidence in the report.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: I've got some questions about that too.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: I guess we consider all studies. What we do is we apply a particular weighting as to what the study shows us. Does it add anything new to the story? Does it shift the regulatory decision that was found in 2016 from the Department of Health's assessment for us on neurotoxicity concerns, and, if so, how does it shift it and what do we need to do in that regard? So on that case—and I think we talked about this, but I was talking in riddles the last time we spoke, because it was about two weeks before we were due to make our decision, so I was circumspect about it. But there's a whole volume of research. A large part of it is drawn off the same dataset of the US Agricultural Health Study, which was set up by the US National Institutes of Health and followed farmers and spouses in Iowa and North Carolina. That's probably the biggest dataset that exists that actually traces and tracks activity and behaviour of farmers and their families and then their health outcomes.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text:
I'll get to some of those studies, but I'm just interested in this one, from reading everything you put out. You seemed happy to point out the shortcomings of studies that showed an association with Parkinson's. You said, 'Oh, well, these things don't'—but then you used this one, which is 30 days, as a study that showed that there was no correlation. I want to turn to your exclusion of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The APVMA's position is 'cited references presenting reviews, opinions, editorials, commentary or clinical opinions or advice' were excluded from detailed review. But, as so many scientists have told me over recent months, systematic reviews and meta-analyses occupy the highest tier of evidence in evidence based medicine and toxicology, and some of the systematic reviews you excluded on the basis that they were reviews, such as Pezzoli and Cereda 2013, pooled and analysed 104 of these studies and concluded two times risk for Parkinson's associated with paraquat exposure.

The thing I really take exception to is that you didn't even apply your own rules uniformly, because the review titled 'Does paraquat cause Parkinson's disease: a review of reviews'—very clearly a review—was included and so was Weed 2024, titled 'A systematic assessment of recent epidemiological evidence'. Neither of these contain original primary data, yet both are cited in your executive summary as supporting the APVMA's conclusions. Why are you excluding reviews that find risks of Parkinson's but you still cite reviews that support your conclusion when you say up the top that you are not going to look at reviews?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

text: The piece that I'm trying to avoid getting here is we don't look at each individual study on its own. It's a weighted evidence of all of the studies that are produced. Every single study that was sent to us is considered and interrogated further, but it adds to the weight of evidence, and that averaging of all of that weight of evidence to arrive at a conclusion is what the key role in a regulatory sense is. So we can go through individual paper by paper, and we intend in our submission to the inquiry to do that in more detail, but it's average weighted evidence that we use to arrive at a determination.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: One of the things that really stuck out from reading your decision is that you point out the shortcomings of studies that don't back up your decision and then you don't do that with ones that do. One academic actually got in touch with me and noted that studies forming the basis of the APVMA's conclusion of no convincing association are largely funded by or written by people connected with Syngenta. There's Smeyne 2016; the author served as a paid consultant to Syngenta. Minnema 2014 was funded by Syngenta and authored by Syngenta employees. Breckenridge 2013 was noted by the APVMA as being a study that was industry supported. There's Vaccari 2019; after the study was finalised, the author became an employee at a private consultancy for pesticide manufacturers. I found this next one very interesting: Weed 2021. The author is from a private consultancy, not actually an academic institution, and his latest papers were titled 'Do cell phones cause brain tumours? Another piece of the puzzle' and 'A metaphor for epidemiology: the sea of person time'. His follow-up piece, Weed 2024, was published in an open-access journal that has been flagged globally by academic institutions as predatory or questionable. This journal charges US$4,000 to publish an article. You have relied on this evidence in your decision. And apart from the Brekenridge one, none of this was mentioned in your summary of studies. Why was there not a note as to who funded these studies? That seems fairly standard practice.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Sorry, Senator and Mr Hansen, it is 9.15. I will let you answer that, and then we do have to take a scheduled break to give the poor hardworking devils behind us a bit of fresh air.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: We are very conscious of the potential for bias in all sources of information that's used in the assessments, and not just bias from the perspective of industry bias. It's always a challenge for us given the fact that it's largely industry who are investing the dollars to do the most detailed analysis and studies, and that's in any of the assessments that we do. But there is also inherent bias in the papers and in the authors who are disease litigation expert witnesses for plaintiffs in court cases. There's a whole series of inherent biases that we acknowledge and look at when we are looking at the papers. But, at the end of the day, it's the data contained within those papers that we look at as well.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: But you didn't acknowledge any of those industry links. That was my question.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Senator Pocock, I did say we went over a little bit. It's not about us; it's about others that need a break too, so we will take it. You will have the call when we come back, but we've still have got seven entities to go. Senator Thorpe has some questions in this space too. So if we can put our minds to that, we can get through them as quick as possible.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Senator Pocock.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Continuing what you were saying earlier, do you accept that industry sponsored research tends to make conclusions that are favourable to industry and that that should probably be noted when you are relying on those studies—that they were funded by the manufacturer?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: We are conscious of the potential for bias in all sources of information that gets provided to us for assessments, and we try to build consideration of that potential into our view. It doesn't mean we discount evidence solely because it's industry funded or solely because it's research that has been done by expert witnesses for court cases; we still look at it. We take into account the potential for bias, but we still look at it. It's an unfortunate scenario that we face in which it's often the industry studies that provide the greater access to the underlying data and the methodologies because, obviously, part of their business is actually collecting the information to support the registration or the continued application for those, as opposed to what might be available in terms of funding and studies that get done by NGOs or others.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text:
I'll put a question on notice about that. I want to ask about some evidence from the Movement Disorder Society of Australia and New Zealand, which is essentially the peak body for neurologists specialising in diseases like Parkinson's. It says:

A robust body of international epidemiological literature demonstrates a consistent, statistically significant association between paraquat exposure and an increased risk of Parkinson's disease:

• In the Farming and Movement Evaluation (FAME) study … every Parkinson's case was individually examined and

confirmed by movement disorder specialist neurologists. FAME established that paraquat exposure is associated

with 2.5 times the odds of developing Parkinson's disease …

• High-resolution spatial studies in California utilising mandatory Pesticide Use Reporting records demonstrate that

living or working within 500 metres of paraquat application sites more than doubles Parkinson's disease odds …

confirming a clear dose-response relationship without retrospective recall bias.

How is it that our country's neurologists are telling us one thing and you are telling us another thing? How is it that there is just are such a divergence? You are telling us that there is no convincing association, while our nation's doctors are saying that the evidence couldn't be stronger.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text:
There are two distinct pieces of studies there—I'll try to be as quick as I can, Chair. The FAME study, which is a really important and valuable contribution in terms of the research, is the work that was done by Tanner in 2011. It looked at that broader US ag health study that I started to talk about before. And it looked for detections of Parkinson's and then did retrospective assessment: 'Tell us your history. What's your recall with regard to—'? And it came up with a odds ratio of 2.5. So it was a really important piece of study.

That same cohort, that same group of data had had work done on it just before in a research paper by Kamel et al. in 2007, and it did an equally important bit where it looked at incident cases and prevalent cases. A prevalent case is where you look at someone with the disease and you ask them to tell you what they have been exposed to or what they've done, and you try to find correlation between that data and the disease they have. That's versus incident cases, in which you collect history and records about someone before they develop the disease. That same cohort, which Tanner used in the FAME study, was the cohort that was used by Kamel. That study also found, I think, that there was about a 1.8 odds ratio, an 80 per cent increase chance, in those who had already had the disease and were being asked to recall what their exposures were to things. In those, in which they had just recorded the information and then had subsequently developed Parkinson's, it was a one. It was a no-correlation piece. And it brought in this importance bit about the recall bias that does come to play. Those two both looked at that.

There have been four or five other really important studies that looked at that same cohort of people and asked things about whether they wore gloves, whether they didn't wear gloves, their genetics—they looked at a whole series of individual pieces. That bigger cohort, though, ended up being that Shrestha study that I continue to struggle to pronounce. He looked at 38,000 applicators and 28,000 of their spouses and followed them for 20 years. He was collecting information and followed up with their health, dealing with the same cohort of people that all those other studies were but in a 10 times magnitude. It was looking at collecting that information in cases in which the disease was not yet prevalent. It's the one that identifies a null conclusion—it goes from a 0.8 through to a one point something, about a 1.09 sort of odds ratio. But they all add to that evidence that we look at, and it's that weight of evidence, about 20 cases versus 490 cases. It's that kind of weighing up that the toxicologists—not the neurologists, but the toxicologists—that work within APVMA and study that relationship between chemicals and populations have been looking at.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: The problem for me, though, is inconsistencies. Because Paul 2024 didn't have recall bias, and yet you discounted it. It was designed not to have recall bias and to establish an individual-level exposure estimate based on distance between their home and their workplace and recorded paraquat applications, but the APVMA dismissed it. You say, 'Well, it had recall bias, and we can't use it. This didn't have recall bias, but we can't use it.' But I just wanted to go to the—

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Sorry, I know I said I was going to comment. That was the scene when we talked about—proximity to places. And this is not recall bias. This is the challenge you get with ecological fallacy about the fact that because something is close to something it must have been exposed to something in a certain way. And this is one of the problems when you don't have any measurements that actually allow you to work out what distance you need to be from something for there to actually be exposure and at what level and, therefore, what the impact might have been. Paul, that study, was another good piece of additional work. The problem is its title. It called itself 'Ambient paraquat exposure' but actually didn't measure ambient paraquat exposure at any of the residences, the workplaces or sources; they merely measured the geospacing from farms and agricultural areas and associated the distance from that to potential pesticide use and proximity to, therefore, exposure. And that's a really challenging piece to try to use in a regulatory sense, to work out whether you can draw a line between exposure and—
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: But that's not ecological fallacy. You are saying it has ecological fallacy, but it established individual-level exposure estimates. And, as one scientist said to me, it does not contain ecological fallacy in the traditional sense. Ecological fallacy describes the attribution of group-level associations to individuals within the group. That's not what that study did.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: No, but it's an assumption that all locations within a given proximity from a point source of a chemical release will have the same exposure regardless of prevailing winds, topography, the point source, the nature of the chemical, the pattern of application—a range of other factors that determine all that. It might not be the same classical definition—apologies if I'm using the wrong shorthand on that—but applying an assumption that a whole series, a whole group or a whole location is equal to each of the individuals is what we are—
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Sure. So what do you want? A double-blind trial where everyone drinks—I want to take you to the statutory test. Section 5A(1)(b) of the Agvet code requires the delegate to be satisfied that use 'is not, or would not be, likely to have an effect that is harmful to human beings'.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: That's right. And if we find that we are satisfied, then we must continue the registration or must vary the labels. If we are not, then we cannot. And that's the test that we end up coming down to. So when we look at this and ask ourselves the question, 'Do we think it's likely, on the weighted evidence we have at the moment,' and I say, 'at the moment'—on the weight of evidence we have at the moment the answer is no.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: So do you need a double-blind trial? What are you waiting for? Seventy countries have done this.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text:
The 70 countries was—I had to look up some of those countries you dropped on me last time to find where they were on the map. Those 70 countries are a really—it's a misleading piece that gives people false hope that there is a single silver bullet on this stuff. In those countries, you've got 27 EU member states that have not continued with paraquat, and that's because of the EU assessment of deficiencies in the regulator's process, not because of actually finding any health concerns; their process was found to be deficient. They sent it back to be reworked and no-one decided to rework it. We have got a whole lot of United Kingdom, Norway—all around high acute toxicity.

This is a really hazardous chemical. Exposure to it dermally—exposure to skin—is nearly fatal. Drinking a teaspoon of it is irreversibly fatal. Many of the countries in that 70 have removed it from their countries because they don't have the same mechanisms around poison scheduling, the control of use that we have here. And, as a result, it was a significant—both accidental and deliberate poisoning risk in those local conditions, and that's why you've got a long list of countries in the Sahel regional band, the Gulf Cooperative Council band.

When we actually look at regulators who have talked about potential linkages between Parkinson's and paraquat, the one who talks about it but doesn't use it as the trigger for their ban was Brazil—out of all of the 70-something that are talked about. The other regulators in the OECD world who have done the regulatory science risk assessment on this, whether it's the Americans, New Zealanders, Canadians—I can't answer your question about what we need to be satisfied, because it is one of those things that will be the weight of what we see in front of us. It won't be one study; it will be the next time we look at this and on the back of additional information that is generated, and I can't say what that would be.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: But what would you need, because—

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Senator Pocock, I'm going to have to ask you to share the call around.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Last one?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Yes.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Thank you. Paul 2024 has been described to me by scientists in this space as a very high powered study. What kind of study would you actually need? What ethics committee would ever approve that sort of study?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Again, I don't know how—
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: I don't know what it would look like. Sorry, Senator.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Senator Thorpe.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Thank you for appearing so late and being patient. I'm just going to follow on from some of the things that Senator Pocock has talked about. One that particularly concerns me is APVMA is the only chemical regulation body in the OECD that has majority funding from the industry. You receive your income from fees, charges and levies from the industries. How do you ensure you make decisions independent of chemical company influence, and how often does APVMA require independent toxicological assessment of a proposed chemical in addition to or instead of industry provided toxicological data?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: A-P-V-M-A.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: A-P-V-M-A. You know what I'm talking about. Thank you.

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text:
Thanks for that question. So we are costs recovered. That's the government policy arrangement for funding of us, and we are funded by fees that the applicants pay upfront and then on a levy, a collection of sale. We do receive government appropriations to assist us with the funding of activities around emergency use permits and minor use permits—that's what's being proposed. But the legislation makes it really clear as to what we can consider and can't consider.

It also puts the emphasis on the applicant to actually provide the information to make sure that we are satisfied as to the legislative requirements that we need to follow to be able to approve a chemical. So it needs to demonstrate that it's safe. It needs to demonstrate it's safe to people, to the environment and to the target, animal or crop that it's being applied to. It needs to demonstrate it's efficacious. It needs to demonstrate the fact that it's not going to unduly influence trade. If it does those things, our legislation means that we have to approve it, and, if it doesn't do those things, then it means we have to refuse it. It's that legislative underpinning that gives us that independence.

Bits have also been added along the way, such as the fact that companies can't just keep drip-feeding information to us to try to get us over the line. With the submission and the package that they give us up the front, the only way they can add additional information to that is if we deliberately ask for it. Anything else they give us we don't take into account, and we arrive at our conclusion based on that package of information that they provide.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Thank you. Australia's PFAS National Environmental Management Plan 3.1, the NEMP 3.1, adopts the OECD definition of PFAS—substances containing at least one fully fluorinated carbon atom—which is the same definition used by the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water. Given many of the newer pesticides are meeting this definition, such as isocycloseram, does the APVMA accept and apply that same OECD NEMP definition of PFAS?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text:
So we actually don't get to consider the classes of chemicals as such. We look at each application, each product, that gets brought to us. So, with isocycloseram, when it gets brought to us, we look at it in its own right, as its own chemical structure, regardless of how many carbon and fluoride atoms it has joined up together. We then look at what else gets mixed in with it in that formulation that it's going to be used in, and we run our environmental and our health assessments on the individual chemicals and that combination of chemicals that are together.

I only say that because, for a number of government agencies, classifications such as what falls into the definition of PFAS is important for their standards and their guidelines. For us, we look at each and every single one of them because they all break down differently. Isocycloseram is a good example. The Americans don't count it, because it doesn't look like a PFAS to start with. But it actually breaks down, and one of its—
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Metabolites.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Metabolites. One of its metabolites is actually a PFAS, and so the European Union and the OECD calls it a PFAS. We look at it as a chemical structure in its own right. I know it's different to how some of our partners in the environment department and partners across in the department of health look at it—with regard to AICIS, the industrial chemical regulator and so forth—but we look at the individual chemicals one by one. Some of them break down quickly and have a relatively short half-life, and some of them hang around forever, and we run different tests for each and every one of those individual chemicals.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Well, PFAS hangs around forever. So, to be clear, you do or don't accept the OECD NEMP definition?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Both definitions have total relevance in terms of what they are trying to look for and what they are trying to do. We don't need to apply it in our sense, because we look at each and every individual chemical itself, regardless of whether it's going to meet the OECD or whether it's going to meet the US definition. We largely rely on OECD guidelines for all of our assessment pieces. So, for example, for all of our environmental assessment of chemicals that are classified as PFAS, we run a European calculator to calculate the risks associated with them. We use a US calculator to help us calculate worker exposure and what the risks are associated with that. So we draw from both, but we look at the individual chemical on its own rather than giving it a label as to whether it's a US or an EU PFAS.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: So you don't use a single definition of PFAS?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: No, because it doesn't really come into our assessments.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: So why should different arms of the government apply different definitions of PFAS to the same chemicals, with the result that a substance may be regulated as a forever chemical by the environment department but not by the pesticides regulator?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Again, it comes down to the fact that we will look at the individual structure of that chemical. We will model what its accumulation in a soil might be for 50 years, and we will say, 'Is it safe to the environment or not?' regardless of which definition it meets, in terms of whether it's classified by the Europeans or the Americans as a PFAS. So, for us, which one of those two is not really a consideration that we take into account in our assessment and modelling; we look at the actual chemical structure of each and every one of these chemicals that gets classified, which means that those government agencies that do need to use a definition of PFAS to work out policies and guidelines—you're right—should all have a singular definition that's used by Australia. I'm just not sure which one it is, because we don't look at it as a PFAS; we look at it as a chemical structure in its own right.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Isocycloseram is a recently registered and now widely sprayed insecticide that meets the OECD NEMP definition of PFAS. This year, APVMA proposed increasing the permitted residues of isocycloseram on berries—a food eaten raw, unpeeled and in quantity by young children—by roughly 70 to 500 times. What consideration did the APVMA give to the persistence and PFAS status of isocycloseram and to cumulative dietary exposure in children, in reaching that proposal?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: Good question. I will see if Mr Deller wants to start off.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: For isocycloseram, the APVMA considered a complete high-quality data package that met the international standards for pesticide residues, both for the registered uses and the use approved under permit, which includes the berry use. So expected residues in food were assessed using Australian consumption data and internationally recognised methods for assessing dietary exposure, both short term and long term. So Food Standards Australia New Zealand, who is our partner in assessing food exposure risks, independently reviewed the dietary exposure assessment, and they agreed that consumer exposure to isocycloseram is acceptable.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text:
Can I just add a couple of things. Maximum residue limits are probably one of the worst named things in terms of trying to explain it to anyone. The maximum residue limit is the maximum amount of residue that is expected to be found in a product if it has been used legally according to label. It is magnitudes away from what a safe level is. In this case we build in a 100-times safety factor to reduce down what the ADI is, which is the acute level exposure—so, if you ate quickly in one day, it might lead to an acute toxicity—or what the acute reference dose is, which gives you that longer term accumulation point that you were just raising.

So we build in a safety margin of over 100 from those numbers and then make sure that the use pattern is going to end up with residues that are nowhere near that safety limit. If it starts to get near that safety limit, we change the rules on the labels. We did that recently, for example, with dimethoate in berries, where we had the same challenge of blueberry consumption increasing significantly, meaning that the number of berries being eaten increased, which started to approach our safety margin—that 100-times safety margin. So we increased the withholding period between spraying and when berries could be picked to further allow time for it to degrade in the berry and be present at a lower level.

I know everyone will have their own view, but the presence of a chemical in foods doesn't necessarily inherently mean it's unsafe. What we do is we consider how much of a product should still be found if—because it's only able to be used if it's going to meet the safety requirements. If it's been used according to the label, how much should it be found so that we can use it as a compliance tool to actually find where people are using it incorrectly or illegally, to be able to use that as a compliance tool to understand and carry out investigations or to help the states carry out those investigations?

That 500-fold increase, for example, was actually moving the treatment time to closer towards the harvest point, which meant that there was a higher amount of the residue in the berry. You might have to remind me, but I think it was 10 per cent of that 100-times safety margin that ended up being as a result of what was in those berries—so still incredibly safe, even when modelled over the long-term exposure that we do in terms of modelling that. It's a difficult thing when you start talking about increasing residues by 500 per cent, though, to sort of get that across.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: It's turning me off berries—that's for sure. So APVMA sets maximum residue limits, or MRLs, for pesticides on food items. Before any MRL can be proposed or established, the APVMA must assess whether expected residues associated with the proposed use pattern are safe for consumers. Am I correct that you assess this and set the MRL in isolation for each pesticide, meaning you do not look at a cumulative effect if a food crop has been sprayed with several pesticides?

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text:
We do look at accumulation effect, and we do look at total exposure within a diet as well. So, for one product, it might be used across 20 different crops, and our calculators assess the potential exposure across that whole diet and builds that into the models that we do, as well as look at the accumulation across a likely diet of chemicals that act and behave in the same way, because those modes of operation might work together to create a risk. So we do look at that.

What we also do, though, is set the MRL for that use pattern. We then present or give all that information across to Food Standards Australia New Zealand, who have shared responsibilities for residues in food. They maintain the Food Standards Code, and that food standards code establishes the legal requirements for any food sold in Australia and New Zealand.

That code actually has a schedule attached to it that specifies the maximum residue limits which are legally permitted in or on any food sold in Australia before an MRL is included in that. So we will do our calculations, we will provide that to FSANZ, and they will do their calculations and assess whether the resulting dietary exposure fits within relevant health based guidance values. And, if it does, then they include that in schedule 20 in their act. If not, then they don't and it is not legally able to be sold in Australia.
witness_organisation: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority

agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: When I wrote a letter to APVMA in July this year about my concerns with the use of PFAS pesticides and whether APVMA assesses for safer alternatives when allowing chemicals on to the market, the response stated that the legislation does not allow the APVMA to undertake comparative assessments between registered products or determine whether alternative technologies may be preferable. agency: Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
text: As far as I see, no-one does that. We regulate and we look at each individual chemical, and we can't take into account or have consideration to whether there's an alternative that's cheaper or an alternative that's safer. We have to look at the merit of that individual application, and again our legislation ties us. If it meets the statutory criteria of safety efficacy, we must register it. If it doesn't, we must not. We don't get to compare it against other things, unfortunately.

We've had an approval in the budget through 2026-27 to increase our average staffing levels from 195 to 222. We've brought in additional contractors to assist us.
