text: I did attempt that, but the director-general of fisheries in Queensland has sent me a copy of the legislation that the federal government passed banning the use of gillnets in fishing. So I think the problem now rests with us as the Commonwealth that's now legislated a ban. Perhaps the department secretary could assist me here. Which one overrides the other? Who wins?

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: Usually the implementation of an international commitment has to be done through domestic law. I'm making an assumption here because I have no personal knowledge of that, but I imagine that ban was effectively implementing an international commitment. We can take that on notice and check with our colleagues in DCCEEW to confirm that.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: I would appreciate that, because there seems to be a great deal of confusion over who has responsibility for this. My concern is that, for this department, it will mean the removal of tonnes and tonnes of fish that's currently available both to the domestic market and to go overseas. We talked earlier today about the food security plan. Given what we import—I think we've got it down to 65 or 70 per cent of the fish that we eat in Australia, an extraordinary number given we're surrounded by ocean—can you point me to where in the food security plan we would be examining our own ability to fish for ourselves?

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: As we talked about this morning, in the production element of the food security strategy we include fisheries. So it's not just about land based farming. I think it would be incorporated in that thinking. Considering what proportion of domestic production we should have in order to support our solid food security would be part of that strategy consideration.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: To just add to the secretary's comments, absolutely the matters you've raised are matters that we are actively considering in relation to the food security strategy. In part, the matters you refer to are in relation to the spatial squeeze question, which is the pressure on the fishery estate. We are working with the CSIRO to better understand where Australia's most productive seafood areas are now and are likely to be in the future. This work is intended to assist government and industry make evidence based decisions about investment and spatial management affecting seafood production.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text:
I think that makes sense—that we'd be examining the viability of our own fishing areas. But I have asked questions previously of Fisheries Research and Development Corporation about the sustainability of the fishing stocks, particularly barramundi, grey tuna and the other fish that have been affected by these impacts, and all of them are considered sustainable. None of them were considered under threat. I am really perplexed. We have such a huge percentage of seafood coming into Australia, we're an island nation surrounded by bountiful waters—I don't think anybody would think we don't—and we have a relatively small population, yet tonight I discover that the Australian Fisheries Management Authority has no knowledge of the legislative change that bans gillnet fishing, a practice that is very highly targeted and well-managed and has almost zero interactions with other species. That is really concerning to me and shocking. I look to you, as an organisation, as being the pre-eminent fish experts in the country, yet you're telling me you don't know the legislation that has banned gillnet fishing in Australia and you don't have knowledge of the data and decision-making around alternative fishing methods. We will potentially lose tonnes and tonnes of Australian-caught fish from our own fisheries and then import more from overseas, from seafood areas that are not well-managed and certainly not to our high standards.

This is, I think, possibly the most talked about issue in Far North Queensland. We have fishing families in tears. We have chandlers, small-boat makers, ice makers who are wondering if they'll survive. I've stood in seafood shops in Ingham, places where pensioners come in and look at the fish, and the prices have already gone up 25 to 30 per cent because of the reductions on the catch that's available to fishers. And here you are, the Commonwealth authority, and you can't discuss this with me.

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: Perhaps I could just add something. I guess AFMA's responsibilities are confined almost entirely to Commonwealth waters, which it is the responsible regulator for. I think the fishery that is in question is a fishery that's managed by the Queensland government, the state of Queensland.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: But the federal government has legislated it, hasn't it?

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: The federal government's legislation, I think, as the secretary has mentioned, is a matter that sits outside our portfolio set of responsibilities and is best directed to another part of government.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: We've talked about this previously tonight. This is, frankly, why Australians are going mad. Anybody listening to this would say, 'How is the agricultural department not across food production from fisheries and this absolutely crazy political decision to shut down gillnet fishing, which is going to affect my ability to get fish and the price I pay?' Australians already import one million tins of tuna and consume it—one million tins of tuna a day. What are we doing about it? Well, we're going to shovel more imported fish into our shops and onto our shelves. It sounds like I'm having a go—and I am having a go—but this is BS, isn't it? This is absolutely the worst of Utopia and government inaction and appalling decision-making. You're the ag department, you're responsible for our food security, and we're all sitting here with our hands on our thumbs going: it's somebody else's problem.

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: Can I help you there, Senator McDonald?

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: Please, Chair, please.

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: I can understand your frustration. It's been a bad couple of days, and, please, I'm just waiting for the answer, but I will plead with my colleagues. We've got—

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: I'm sorry, Chair

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: Can we get to them or can we release them?

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: I reckon you can release the Inspector-General of Biosecurity.

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text:
Thank you very much. I appreciate that, Senator Cadell. Regional Investment Corporation and Inspector-General of Biosecurity, I'm sorry it took so long but it's not the fault of the committee; there are a lot of people who've come in. Thank you very much.

Senator McDonald, you had asked the question. Mr Lowe, do you want to have a—

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: Certainly. Chair, as you've expressed, we appreciate your frustration in relation to the matter. We are concerned ourselves. Our primary responsibility in relation to fisheries is in relation to Commonwealth fisheries as well, not state fisheries. As you mentioned, there are states' rights, we do live in a federation and we do have to respect those constitutional boundaries. We are cognisant of that. The matter that you referred to, though, does concern us. We certainly, as a starting point, think that an important policy development has been the introduction of mandatory country-of-origin labelling for seafood in food service establishments. I think the first thing you can do is ensure that consumers are aware whether it's been produced from Australia, whether it's imported or whether it's mixed, and that's what the policy intervention has done. I think arming consumers with that information so they can make a choice about what's locally produced is an important starting point.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: It is, but unfortunately all we will be telling them is whether or not it's come from Indonesia or the Philippines or China or some other place. It will just be which foreign place it's come from. So the feds have done two things that we should hang our heads in shame on. The first is that we've increased the zone and the NX fishing area. The second is that we have legislated over states' rights, states' responsibilities, because it's not just in Commonwealth waters; it's being implemented in inshore fishing zones. I will leave it there, Chair. But this is absolutely appalling decision-making and I look forward to following up with you with those questions on notice.

agency: Australian Fisheries Management Authority
text: Thank you, Senator.
witness_organisation: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Policy Group

agency: Fisheries Research and Development Corporation

agency: Fisheries Research and Development Corporation

agency: Fisheries Research and Development Corporation
text: Certainly, the intention was for it to look at those overlaps and quantify where there were displacements and potential interactions that would need to be managed. That was one of the intentions of the work. I'd need to go and have a look at the specifics of each of those zones, but it's not the only area where the zones are proposed. Where I'm based, in Port Stephens on the east coast in New South Wales—
witness_organisation: Fisheries Research and Development Corporation

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: Welcome. Senator Canavan?

text: I have some questions on the Livestock Product Assurance accreditation system. I believe this is put out by the Integrity System Company organisation. You've got some responsibility for that?

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: Yes. It's a wholly owned subsidiary of MLA.
witness_organisation: Meat and Livestock Australia

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text:
That accreditation includes a number of questions that livestock producers have to fill out. I'm particularly interested in question 2.8, which reads:

Do livestock have access to leaking electrical transformers, capacitors, hydraulic equipment, solar panels, wind turbines, coal seam gas structures or coal mine wastes?

Why are solar panels and wind turbines a risk to a product assurance system relating to food safety?

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: The question was included in LPA around the increase in renewable energy installations on farms, and it was more not to deter people to do that at all. There's certainly no restriction on solar farms or wind farms on farm. It's more about just keeping an eye on ageing infrastructure and, if there are any risks identified, that they are raised as part of the LPA accreditation.
witness_organisation: Meat and Livestock Australia

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text:
Right. Your own advice does say there are potential risks 'associated with livestock exposure to persistent chemicals, pathogens from recycled water or physical infrastructure.' Quoting directly there from your guidance to producers, it goes on to say:

This includes access to renewable energy infrastructure, including solar panels and wind turbines, particularly as they degrade with age.

So exactly what are the chemicals or pathogens that are exposed to livestock from degrading solar panels and wind turbines?

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: I'm not sure, Senator. I'll have to come back to you on that.
witness_organisation: Meat and Livestock Australia

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: If you could take that on notice. Has the Integrity Systems Company relied on any particular studies here to conclude that there are risks from wind and solar panels to livestock production?

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: I'll come back to you on that. It's also important to note that we have a dedicated supply chain taskforce where we work with peak industry bodies on any changes to the LPA program as well. There was also consultation with industry included in any of those changes to LPA, but I'll come back to you on the detail.
witness_organisation: Meat and Livestock Australia

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: Given this advice, the Integrity Systems Company does accept that solar panels and winds turbines do pose a contamination risk to livestock?

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: It's more flagging that, as producers have these installations on farm, they monitor if there are any risks with having those installations on farm as they age.
witness_organisation: Meat and Livestock Australia

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: Does this risk have to be declared on an NVD?

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: No, it doesn't.
witness_organisation: Meat and Livestock Australia

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: Why not?

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: Because, I think, generally speaking, it's a very low risk. It is not something that is identified at the moment as a food safety concern.
witness_organisation: Meat and Livestock Australia

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: Are there other risks to contamination from pathogens or chemicals included on the NVD, like coal mine waste or coal seam gas?

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: No.
witness_organisation: Meat and Livestock Australia

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: That's not included either. Okay. If livestock are contaminated, who is ultimately liable?

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: That's a good question, again, in that we would have to go back to the state and territory jurisdictions on that.
witness_organisation: Meat and Livestock Australia

agency: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited
text: Moving on, I believe NLIS 2.0 has a revised go-live target. What's caused the delay?

agency: Dairy Australia
text: Welcome. Thank you, gentlemen. Sorry about the lateness, but it could always be worse; you could be doing four days of it! Do you want to make a very brief opening statement before we go to coalition questions?

text: Earlier in the day, we were talking about milk. We were talking about dairy and how we're going on the food security plan there. Given our herd size is maintaining but not increasing, and a number of farmers are out, how are you working with the industry? Anecdotally, they were saying that dairy farm profits seem up a little bit now, but being a dairy farmer is the toughest gig I've ever heard of. There's still industry about the $1.20 milk. They're still going around a push for the $2 milk. How are we involved in keeping the industry strong when we've got such internal stressors, when we see EU trade adoption with big subsidies on European dairy products coming here? What can we do as government? What should we looking to do?

agency: Dairy Australia
text: There are two parts I look at with our dairy profitability. It's obviously the price, but we work on the cost end with our productivity. As far as—

text: There's a lot of diesel in the transporting, isn't there?

agency: Dairy Australia
text: There is. On the farm side and on the transport side, there's a lot of diesel and those sorts of things involved in that cost. I guess our focus is on the cost of production and more of the productivity and what we're trying to achieve on farm. There are a number of ways we're looking to do that and sharpen in with our new strategic plan; I'll get Matt to talk a little bit more about some of the key elements. As far as productivity goes, it has been an upward trend for the dairy industry on a per-cow and per-farm basis. Whilst we have a lot fewer dairy farmers, those farmers and those cows are far more productive than they were 10 to 20 years ago.
witness_organisation: Dairy Australia

agency: Dairy Australia
text: Everything's two milks a day now.

agency: Dairy Australia
text: Just a little snapshot on some of that is the work that we've done in our genetics space, and a lot of that has been industry and farmer funded. That's a huge productivity gain in what we're seeing with our genetics with our animals now. That's part of what we're looking at. So, yes, we've got more productive farms but fewer of them. On the profitability side of things, it's very much driven by seasons as well as price. We've seen quite a good season, particularly coming off a really bad one the year before in the south where the engine room of our milk production is. We have seen a better season that's driven more profitability.
witness_organisation: Dairy Australia

agency: Dairy Australia
text: I thought you were going to chime in there.

agency: Dairy Australia
text: Sure, just to simply say that Dairy Australia focuses on the productivity side. We're helping farmers make different decisions on how to be productive on their farms. To be clear, it doesn't mean this guy has to work harder; it just means that they sweat their assets a bit more, and we try to help them do that through our investments in everything from training people through genetics, as Paul says, and also the forges.

agency: Dairy Australia
text: When you look at the productivity stuff, getting fewer farmers but bigger farms helps on the capital outlay. text: Welcome. Do you wish to make a brief opening statement?

agency: Grains Research and Development Corporation
text: In the essence of time, I won't.

agency: Grains Research and Development Corporation
text: Great, thank you. Senator Cadell.

agency: Grains Research and Development Corporation
text: I think last time we talked about this. What does GRDC's reserves policy set the target at, and why are reserves so far above it in your cash balances?

agency: Grains Research and Development Corporation
text:
I might start by talking about where the reserves are, and then I'll hand over to Mr Hart to talk about our reserves policy. Our reserves, as of the end of June of this year, as reported in our annual report, are sitting at $815 million. To provide some greater context around that figure, though, we need to take into consideration that GRDC has over $600 million worth of forward contracts or commitments. The board has been very conscious in thinking about the reserves, and the reserves serve two purposes. One is that, as with any agricultural industry, there is higher variability in seasons. We only need to go back to 2019, when there was an expansive drought across grain-growing areas across Australia, and GRDC had to make some cuts and reductions in terms of their investment around R&D.

The other purpose of reserves is that it does allow the organisation to invest in much longer term projects, projects that are going to be delivered over a 10-year period and that, in basic science, are going to answer some of the big questions. For example, one of the announcements that GRDC did make over the last 12 months was a nitrogen mission. Nitrogen fertilisers are really key inputs for any farming business as a grower. We've seen our fertiliser prices increasing somewhere between 30 and 50 per cent, so they are a significant input cost in our business. The nitrogen fertiliser mission aims to look at transformational ways or investing in new science which will give us step changes in nitrogen management on farm. Our reserves actually enable us to do that by investing over a 10-year timeframe and attracting the best and most talented people and researchers to actually develop these solutions to growers.
witness_organisation: Grains Research and Development Corporation

agency: Grains Research and Development Corporation
text: I've only got a minute left; we will stop at 11.00. I've got some other financial questions I'll put on notice. What research are you funding on phosphine fumigation at the moment under the new exposure limit, if any, and when will any of that come out?

text: Yes, we are. We stood up a project in which we are investing about $7.4 million over three years. We are confident—well, not confident, but we are certainly going to be ensuring that we invest in a way in which we can help to—again, the challenge with the new phosphine levels is there's no current technology that can actually measure it. So our job is really to try and develop that technology to measure it to those levels, and that's what the purpose of the R&D is.
witness_organisation: Grains Research and Development Corporation

On saying that, can I take this opportunity to sincerely thank my Senate colleagues.
